EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:34:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Czech MEP Markéta Gregorová stopped at Chinese border in ‘pseudo-scare tactics’ https://euobserver.com/246452/czech-mep-marketa-gregorova-stopped-at-chinese-border-in-pseudo-scare-tactics/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:04:19 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246452 MEP Markéta Gregorová claims to have been stopped in Beijing in what she called “pseudo-scare tactics” over the arrest of a Chinese national accused of spying in Czech Republic.]]> Czech Greens/EFA MEP Markéta Gregorová claims to have been detained in Beijing for 1.5 hours in what she called “pseudo-scare tactics” over the arrest of a Chinese national accused of spying in the Czech Republic.

Gregorová said she was the only delegate out of 15 EU officials who faced such problems at border control upon landing in Beijing Capital Airport on Monday (26 October).

A vocal critic of the Chinese Communist Party, Gregorová said she faced extensive questioning from Chinese officials despite presenting her diplomatic passport and an official invitation letter.

Gregorová is the vice-chair of the European Parliament’s China group, and was travelling to the Chinese capital as part of a delegation from the parliament focusing on trade talks between Brussels and Beijing.

The visit follows recent talks between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese officials.

Gregorová claims she was banned from using her phone during the ordeal and had her passport confiscated.

]]> Listen: What’s at stake for Europe in the US midterms? https://euobserver.com/246416/listen-whats-at-stake-for-europe-in-the-us-midterms/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:46:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246416 Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate and according to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below:

Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate. According to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.

What would a Democratic win actually change for Europeans? First, a quick word on what to expect tonight. Polls suggest a win for the Democrats camp, especially in the House of Representatives. 

It is actually common for the president’s party to lose ground at the midterms. And Donald Trump’s approval ratings have been falling steadily.

So, if the Democrats do win, what could they do? Quite a lot, on paper at least. Congress holds significant powers. The House can, for instance, launch impeachment proceedings against the president. But removing him from office would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is very hard to reach.

The Democrats have said they would open investigations into the administration, including on corruption. They want to keep financial support for Ukraine in place, and to end the war in Iran. They also want to roll back many of the tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

Read more

THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

These are all issues of great importance for Europe. But could the Democrats really undo them?

For several of these issues, a simple majority is enough to pass a law. So on that front, they could take a stand. But there is a catch: the president has a veto.

And to override this veto, Congress needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers. In the House, that means around 290 seats. And even in the most optimistic polls, the Democrats don’t get there.

Those polls currently point to a tight race for the Senate, and a more comfortable Democratic win in the House.

Of course, these are estimates to be taken with a pinch of salt. The BBC reminded us yesterday that polls in the United States regularly get it wrong, although they do so less often for midterms.

Read more

Trump, Rubio and Hegseth are fumbling Ukraine – Europe needs to stop making the same mistake

In any case, a two-thirds majority looks like an unlikely scenario. Still, this doesn’t mean nothing will change. The Democrats would still have some levers if they do win.

They could, for example, block bills by simply refusing to vote for them. And they could hold up the budget, and with it, the funding of the war effort.

In the case of the tariffs, the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Donald Trump had overstepped his powers since Congress had not approved the tariffs. This is already a difficulty, even if, for now, the government is playing with the legal basis of the tariffs. 

So, to sum up: the Democrats wouldn’t be able to overturn Donald Trump’s policies altogether, but they could make his life a lot harder.

]]> Andrew Tate’s toxic legacy in Romania is warping its democracy https://euobserver.com/246239/andrew-tates-toxic-legacy-in-romania-is-warping-its-democracy/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:17:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246239 While prosecutors chase the Tates across borders, their macho fantasy of domination is already shaping how a frustrated generation of Romanian men sees women and democracy itself.]]> Prosecutors in Romania officially charged social media influencers Andrew and Christian Tate with trafficking and sex offences involving minors on 4 September. But the Tates were not around to be hauled into a police station in Bucharest – they were in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK on similar charges.

That two of the world’s most high-profile misogynists may finally be brought to justice is a reason to celebrate. But in the country which hosted them for so many years, their toxic legacy continues to pollute the atmosphere.

Why did the Tates choose Romania in the first place?

Before his arrest Andrew Tate expressed a preference for countries where “corruption is accessible to everybody.” 

An underregulated webcam industry and struggles with combating sex trafficking could also be contributing factors.

But this only partially explains why the self-styled ‘king of toxic masculinity’ may have based himself here since 2017, and why his poisonous messages had fertile ground in which to germinate.

Once we understand that, we might be able to start pushing back before it’s too late. 

Read more

Why AI-turbocharged misogyny and porn are threats to EU democracy

Compared to other countries in the region, Romania’s feminist movement is relatively young.

A fertile ground for toxic masculinity

In 2000, the Romanian edition of Playboy published a supposedly satirical article titled: “How to Beat Your Wife Without Leaving Marks.”

The outrage prompted the first major waves of protests and women’s rights activism against gender-based violence and its normalisation in Romanian society.

But in 2026, Romania ranks low in European rankings on gender equality metrics, and high on incidents of domestic violence.

Romania has no mandatory gender equality education and no comprehensive sex education, while across swathes of the country, boys and young men lack access to quality education and jobs.

Successive governments have failed to improve their circumstances, and traditional, social pressure on men to provide for a family or partner fosters anger and resentment.

The manosphere’s appeal

This disillusioned generation presents ripe pickings for demagogues like the Tates to sell a cartoonish fantasy of success based on subjugating women. 

Because of lack of any national data, our organisation helped conduct the first nationally representative study into how rapid social and technological advances are reshaping the values, gender perceptions, and political choices of young Romanian men.

Our findings show a mixed picture where patriarchal beliefs endure but alongside self-confidence issues over how to bond with women.

While 53 percent strongly agree that “in a relationship, a woman should be available for sex whenever her partner wants it,” a slightly higher percentage believe that women still do not have adequate rights. 

The dividing lines are not created by age or urban versus rural but by education and economic precariousness.

A quarter of respondents with university education agree that a man’s honour must be defended through violence, a figure that rises to 50 percent by those with vocational education.

Whereas formal education covering these issues is absent, the online environment fills the vacuum and the misogynistic, racist, and homophobic values of the manosphere connect to extreme-right movements in Romania and worldwide.

Our concerns are that the Tates’ legacy on the minds of young people is so damaging that we may only see the true effects in years to come.

A better model of masculinity

But it is never too late to act. In April, Romanian parliament overwhelmingly supported a new law defining the concept of femicide with offenders given potential life sentences.

The legislation also calls for teaching on gender equality and non-violent relationships to be included in the national curriculum, though this is yet to be implemented.

Many young men are still open to alternative ideas, so we have time to shape their attitudes and we should not delay – 72 percent interviewed agree democracy is a good form of government but 58 percent want a strong leader who does not bother with parliament or elections. 

As a riposte to the commercial masculinity bootcamps run by manosphere characters, our organisation runs free and healthy masculinity camps for young men between 18 to 22 years old.

Led mostly by male trainers, participants from across the country and from a broad socioeconomic background discuss their ideas of masculinity, democracy, extremism, and mental health.

Many describe loneliness, a lack of physical spaces to build friendships, and a growing guilt for being male.

Providing young men with a non-judgmental environment to open up is a better way to ensure a safer society, rather than putting the onus on women to change their behaviour. 

Young men also need to be taught media literacy, so they can recognise hate speech and radicalisation techniques used by the manosphere and the far right to target them.

Positive male role models can encourage young men to open up about problems, but they also need to be exposed to narratives instilling the values of democracy and pluralism.

Online platforms remain vastly under-regulated, while offline spaces that provide young people, male and female, with environments in which to socialise and form meaningful connections are lacking. 

Politicians have successfully harvested the Tates’ audience through skilled social-media targeting, and this bore fruit in the last presidential elections, where young men voted heavily for parties headed by authoritarian leaders.

The radical right is currently leading the polls, and ongoing political deadlock may yet result in them entering government.

Young Romanian men are not yet a lost cause, but without a concerted societal effort to combat the sinister forces that influence them, democracy in Romania, and across Europe, may not survive their loss.

A new study reveals the extent of those Frontex-assisted interceptions, totalling some 33,000 between 2018 and 2024.]]> Aerial surveillance by the EU’s border agency Frontex over the central Mediterranean has directly led to the interception and return of over 33,000 people to Libya and Tunisia between late 2018 and 2024.

The findings, revealed on Tuesday (3 November) by the EU-funded Liminal project, comes as the Warsaw-based Frontex is set to get more deportation powers and greater pre-frontier intelligence gathering capabilities.

“In 2021, the year with the most complete data available, detection by Frontex’s aircraft accounted for at least 36 percent of all recorded pushbacks,” according to Liminal.

The agency has already allocated €330m for aerial surveillance for 2027 with the European Commission demanding an additional €169m for drones, seaborne equipment and state-of-the-art high-altitude systems.

In July, the agency flew its largest drones from a ship at sea, extending the reach and range of the surveillance as part of test pilot with Italy.

Money and policy aside, Liminal’s findings also put into sharp relief how the EU over the years has created a system that obscures legal responsibility, turns Libya and Tunisia into EU anti-migrant police proxies and piles increasing pressure onto charity rescue vessels to stop saving people.

Read more

On an Italian dock, the EU’s new asylum pact gives rescued migrants a rushed ‘tick-box’ border screening

The legal obfuscation includes helping bankroll and set up Libya’s rescue zone, which now regularly sees aggressive Libyan coast guard boats well into areas normally patrolled by Malta.

Liminal says they identified 16 cases in which Frontex aerial assets detected a migrant boat but did not directly alert nearby charity ships able to help.

The agency broadcasts alerts on public radio frequencies, which can be received by anyone within range of transmission.

Karol Nawrocki had even turned back mid-flight from a planned visit to Senegal and went into the Tribunal’s building, pushing aside a judge who had blocked the door.

Together with his own guards and aides, Nawrocki stayed in the premises until the early morning hours, as a few thousand protesters camped outside.

And leaving in the morning, he thanked them for having “defended the Polish constitution.”

The events unfolded amid a clash between the centre-right prime minister Donald Tusk and the rightwing opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), supporting Nawrocki, over the status of judges in the country’s highest court.

And the PiS party’s approach to the situation was “designed to heighten perceptions of existential political conflict and mobilise supporters,” while making Tusk look like part of an unaccountable elite, said Roch Dunin-Wąsowicz, a politics professor at University College London.

Natasza Styczyńska, a scholar of European studies at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, also told EUobserver that the courtroom melodrama was meant to “strengthen the image” of PiS ahead of next year’s parliamentary election, which falls due by 11 November.

]]> Scandal-hit EU innovation agency disputes auditors’ finding that €8.7m may be unrecoverable https://euobserver.com/246128/scandal-hit-eu-innovation-agency-disputes-auditors-finding-that-e8-7m-may-be-unrecoverable/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:46:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246128 The European Institute of Innovation & Technology is under renewed scrutiny after an audit suggested “a material level of error” and flagged that it could fail to recover €8.7m from its beneficiaries. This comes after several investigations into the agency were launched in recent years.]]> The European Institute of Innovation & Technology (EIT), which received €435m in taxpayer money in 2025, is the only EU agency out of a total of 43 whose accounts did not yield a “clean opinion” in the most-recent audit.

The accounts of the innovation hub did not properly reflect an €8.7m recovery uncertainty, according to a report by European Court of Auditors (ECA) last week.

Several dozen of its auditors check the EU agencies every year to form a basis for Brussels bodies to later make decisions on funding.

The financial audit delivers the latest blow to the EIT, an EU agency whose bodies have faced several investigations over spending.

“Taxpayers should be concerned,” said Kenneth Haar, researcher at Corporate Europe Observatory, a watchdog. “I find it amazing and worrying to see the EIT house is still not in order, though it was more than two years ago that investigators first stepped in.”

Lead ECA auditor Petri Sarvamaa said, “The good news is that public money is managed well overall. But the weaknesses we identified also show why strong checks are essential in protecting EU taxpayers’ money.”

Based in Budapest, the EIT aims to boost European competitiveness by connecting enterprises, researchers and education.

It distributes funds to sector-specific partnerships called knowledge and innovation communities (KICs). And the spending habits of some of these KICs have caused a financial and reputational headache for EIT bosses.

Agency disputes €8.7m figure

The ECA’s report of the EIT’s financial accounts published on Thursday (29 October) said the innovation hub’s grant payments were affected by “a material level of error”.

But because verification checks were incomplete, it “could not provide an estimated error rate” of grant payments.

The report also flagged that the agency could fail to recover €8.7m. At least some of this is due to EIT Manufacturing, a KIC which filed for liquidation in March 2026.

The audit states: “An impairment should have been recognised […] EIT receivables and net assets are overstated by €8.7m, impairment expenses are understated by the same amount, and the economic result for the year is overstated by €8.7m.”

But the innovation and tech agency disagreed with these findings.

While the EIT acknowledged that an impairment should have been recognised, it told auditors the amount is actually up to €0.5m, not €8.7m. The chance of recovering the money, the EIT said, is “very likely”.

Specifically, it expects to recover €5.9m via the so-called Mutual Insurance Mechanism (MIM), and €2.3m by offsetting money owed by EIT Manufacturing.

The court of auditors also said risks are “amplified” by the use of multiannual grants reported and cleared only every 18 months. In response, the EIT said it is moving to 12-month reporting periods.

“I think this is all about the pitfalls of letting private actors handle public money, and with relatively few strings attached…. it invites the sort of trouble we have seen,” added Haar.

“At another level, I believe it is a symptom of the laissez-faire approach of the EU institutions to start-ups and innovation.”

Read more

EU’s Horizon-suspension sanction for Israel ‘a bad joke’, says Borrell

Pumped up KICs?

EU law sets out that in their seventh year, KICs should be subject to scrutiny before they can receive another seven years of taxpayer money.

They are envisioned to become financially independent and sustainable after 15 years of existence.

In 2025, the digital, clean energy, and climate change KICs were due to be independent as they reached their 15th birthdays. 

But in 2026-27 two of them reportedly received a shared total of €43m from the EIT, which pumped up KICs with EU funds past the supposed expiration date.

    ]]>         On an Italian dock, the EU’s new asylum pact gives rescued migrants a rushed ‘tick-box’ border screening https://euobserver.com/246241/on-an-italian-dock-the-eus-new-asylum-pact-gives-rescued-migrants-a-rushed-tick-box-border-screening/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:04:44 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246241 The impact of the EU's new pact on migration and asylum is clearly visible from an Italian port quay on the day of a migrant disembarkation. First touching land after having survived a sail aboard an overcrowded dinghy in a storm, 28 migrants were trooped through a sped-up "tick-boxing" screening, which experts worry will not accurately measure the vulnerabilities they're up against. ]]> The survivors of a recent maritime migrant rescue operation carried out by the German NGO SOS Humanity were screened on the port docks as they first set foot on EU soil, revealing the insensitive efficiency at the centre of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    The reception policies from the pact, implemented in June 2026, require an initial screening of new EU arrivals to last a maximum of seven days. 

    The 28 survivors rescued from an overcrowded dinghy on a stormy night in the central Mediterranean were disembarked at 11 am on Saturday (31 October), and had finished being processed by the evening.

    Under the new pact, that means their asylum decision will have been most likely conducted then and there. 

    The platform alongside the Humanity 1 vessel was bustling with hazmat suits and police. In the northern Italian port of Livorno, a makeshift processing centre was set up to host the Red Cross’s health scan, the EU agency for asylum’s vulnerability scan and legal information session, as well as the police’s interrogation – all to be carried out within hours of migrants’ stunned arrival.

    “Immediately after a rescue, when people only need to rest, they sit through a compressed screening for authorities to rush through a tick-boxing exercise,” said Marta [the NGO requests only first names are used by journalists], SOS Humanity’s protection officer, as survivors from the ship’s rescue were being disembarked by authorities.

    She had prepared vulnerability certificates for those most in need, in the hope their case be treated with more care. 

    “Some border interrogations can become violent, a person has just disembarked and they are suddenly facing hours of interrogations,” Marta told EUobserver. She has often seen armed Frontex or Europol officers standing along the ship at port, towering over migrants in their most vulnerable hours.

    The new pact on migration foresees police registration into Eurodac, a database set up to share information with other member states, followed by an immediate decision as to whether a newcomer should qualify for an accelerated asylum procedure. 

    That means those from nationalities less likely to be granted asylum would receive an answer within 12 weeks, and are most probably going to be rejected.

    Read more

    ‘Let me die’: tortured migrants and rescue ships face off against EU-sponsored Libyan forces

    “There’s no way you can do an accurate screening of all the traumas someone on this journey has lived in 10 minutes with a police officer,” she added.

Catalogue it under “fiction”, writes Edward Lucas.]]> Since the late 1940s, a clique of influential Americans has hijacked their country’s foreign policy to settle personal and family grudges, using Ukraine as a weapon. The result, as avoidable as it was predictable, has been the disaster of Russia’s invasion.

    That is the argument put forward by Stephen Kinzer in Boiling Point: How America brought war to Ukraine.

    He opens with the disastrous clandestine operations that started in 1949, aimed at supporting the underground anti-communist resistance in Ukraine and other countries.

    They were the work of Frank Wisner, a CIA boss traumatised by witnessing the communist seizure of power in Romania. Other villains include Zbigniew Brzezinski (the son of a Polish diplomat), Madelaine Albright (daughter of a Czechoslovak one) and Victoria Nuland, who has family roots in Moldova and (by marriage) Lithuania.

    Like the others, Kinzer argues, “she imbibed anti-Russian passion with her mother’s milk”.

    So what did countries actually agree on? First, they agreed on the diagnosis I just mentioned: that countries are behind on their 2030 goals. That alone was already a fight.

    Women make up 19.5 percent of information and communication technology specialists in the EU. Start-ups with at least one woman founder receive 12 percent of venture capital.

    Women face greater exposure to AI taking over their tasks, are less represented among the people who build the systems, and are under-financed as founders.

    Our task force within the Connecting Women in Digital Forum asked a narrow question: where does AI policy risk leaving women out, and which instruments already in motion could change that?

    We found five gaps

    Nobody has defined a good AI job. The EUCommission could do so, across wages, security, autonomy, progression and voice, in the Quality Jobs Act due later this year.

    Member states also have until 2 December to transpose the Platform Work Directive, whose safeguards on algorithmic management are a ready model they can choose to extend beyond platform work.

    Transition support follows territories, while AI exposure follows tasks. An administrative worker in a region with no designated just transition territory gets nothing. The next EU budget could make occupational exposure an eligibility trigger, with recipients reported by sex.

    European support for women founders stops at a €75,000 grant. Nothing covers the step from there to €2m. The Commission’s Startup and Scaleup Strategy does not even name that gap; the only one it acknowledges sits above €100m. The Action Plan for women in research, innovation and start-ups, still to be adopted, should include a dedicated facility.

    Digital Decade reporting counts adoption, not who benefits. Every AI indicator should be paired with a result reported by sex, starting with the December revision of the national roadmaps.

    The fifth gap is procurement and it sits at the centre of a debate the EU is already having.

    Read more

    Revealed: New data shows Big Tech lobbying pushing EU towards sweeping data-protection rollback

    Europe’s conversation about technological sovereignty usually begins with infrastructure: compute, chips, cloud and data centres. Sovereignty is also produced through purchasing: public contracts decide which suppliers gain revenue, references, scale and credibility.

    In concentrated AI and cloud markets, one significant public contract is often what qualifies a firm to compete for the next.

    Public procurement accounts for around 14 percent of EU gross domestic product. The commission’s proposal for a Public Procurement Act, tabled on 9 September, treats that spending explicitly as strategy: simpler rules, but also environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations, and a European preference.

    It tracks awards to small and medium-sized enterprises, but it does not track awards to women-led firms.

    Start counting the women

    The Cloud and AI Development Act, tabled in June, repeats the pattern: Article 33 requires member states to monitor cloud and AI procurement for barriers facing smaller firms and to report annually on their share of contracts, but it says nothing about gender.

    Adding women-led firms to that reporting requirement would begin to show who is actually winning Europe’s cloud and AI business.

    Procurement data is not currently broken down by technology category or supplier ownership, so policymakers can count contract value without knowing who got the opportunity.

    In one version of sovereignty, Europe could spend more public money on AI and end up reinforcing a concentrated supplier market. In another version, public demand could deliberately broaden the range of firms that can build and scale technology in Europe.

    Both count as European procurement in the statistics, yet they do not produce the same market.

    Importantly, no one needs to wait for the new Act. Article 67  permits contracting authorities to use award criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract, while Article 70 allows conditions governing contract performance. That means a contracting authority can, for example, assess the inclusiveness of the team delivering a contract, where that criterion is sufficiently linked to the contract itself, or require prime contractors to report the share of subcontracted value going to women-led firms.

    Spain has legislated equality criteria across every phase of procurement in its science system, and the European Institute for Gender Equality publishes a methodology. The new Act should add a duty to report awards to women-led firms by number and value, so policymakers can see whether those options are actually being used.

    AI does not need a separate equality regime.

    Each gap we identified can be addressed through an instrument already in force or on the table.

    What is missing is not another framework, but action and political will power. So our ask to EU institutions, and to the governments now transposing, budgeting and negotiating these files, is simple: pick one of the five gaps, name the instrument that can close it, and name who in your institution can act on it immediately.

    ]]>         Kursk and Krynky operations were disasters for Ukraine, new casualty figures show (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,709) https://euobserver.com/246038/kursk-and-krynky-operations-were-disasters-for-ukraine-new-casualty-figures-show-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1709/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:19:44 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246038 Ukraine also targeted a Russian refinery producing fuel for the army and aviation. A massive fire broke out.]]>
  • Confirmed Ukrainian military losses have exceeded 220,000, while the share of missing personnel is rising.
  • Ukraine lost thousands of personnel both during the Kursk region operation and in the battle for Krynky.
  • Following an unofficial pause, Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries — and with considerable success.
  • Ukraine claims to have hit another two Russian Su-34 aircraft. Russia has suffered too many such losses over the past two months.
  • Videos of the day: a report on a soldier who operates drones with his chin; a welcome for Ukraine’s ombudsman in Oleshky.

    • In Ukraine Battlefield update, we report fairly regularly on the enormous losses suffered by Russian soldiers. The Ukrainian command publishes them daily. This figure is probably inflated, but it shows a trend. And that trend shows that October is already the bloodiest month since the start of the full-scale invasion.

    Verified figures are also published by the independent Russian outlets Mediazona and the Russian BBC. The problem is that they can only verify these figures retrospectively, while the Russian state is placing ever more obstacles in their way as they seek information about deaths.

    As Dima Treshchanin wrote, the author of the project, they are currently working on deaths from the summer of 2025.

    However, we devote less attention to Ukrainian military losses. Unfortunately, these are also high.

    However, when independent analysts examined its data, they found it credible. Each entry links to a source of information on a Ukrainian website, mostly an obituary, and the analysts did not find many duplicates either.

    Ukrainian losses are tracked by the UA Losses project. It is an anonymous website and its background is a mystery. Ukrainian authorities describe it as propaganda and have blocked access to its website in Ukraine.

    UA Losses has updated its data in recent days.

      <description><p>Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks</p><p>The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.</p><p>Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/02/oil-price-falls-amid-hope-of-a-breakthrough-to-end-iran-war">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history</p><p>Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jan/03/tesla-diner-elon-musk-los-angeles">Tesla Diner in Los Angeles</a>, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.</p><p>Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/31/elon-musk-midterms-spending-visualized">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/30/tech-stocks-drop-earnings-report</link>
      <description><p>Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough</p><p>A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.</p><p>The S&amp;P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/30/tech-stocks-drop-earnings-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/02/europe-supermarket-fridges-freezers-who-hacking-why">Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?</a></p></li></ul><p>Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.</p><p>Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/02/supermarket-freezers-across-europe-hit-by-second-suspected-cyber-attack">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 03 Nov 2026 11:36:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Ryanair pilots’ union rejects suggestion of pay freeze ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/ryanair-pilots-union-rejects-suggestion-of-pay-freeze-next-year-as-fuel-costs-soar/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/ryanair-pilots-union-rejects-suggestion-of-pay-freeze-next-year-as-fuel-costs-soar/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Ryanair is warning the Irish Airline Pilots’ Association (Ialpa) and other unions that have yet to sign new pay deals that they risk possible salary freezes if they do not reach an agreement with the airline before next April.

However, Ialpa has rejected the suggestion that pilots should accept pay freezes as a result of rising fuel costs.

Faced with a €2 billion fuel bill increase in 2027, the airline is considering cuts across its business that chief executive Michael O’Leary said could include pay freezes where unions have not struck deals with the company by April.

Ex-Munster rugby star’s company eyes €360m aviation fuel investment

Ryanair negotiates multiyear settlements with its unions and recently reached agreements in most of Europe, barring the Republic, United Kingdom, Spain and Portugal, O’Leary confirmed on Monday.

Organisations that have yet to sign deals with the company have the opportunity to do so before Ryanair’s next financial year begins in April, he added.

“We’re not minded to give any pay increases from April next year,” said O’Leary.

If industrial action results, the airline will manage this, O’Leary predicted. “We’re not encouraging strikes, but they will actually save us money,” he said.

Ialpa rejected that pilots should accept pay freezes as a result of rising fuel costs.

“Other airlines manage the same fuel costs while paying their pilots significantly more than those in Ryanair,” the union said.

Noting that the company made a €2 billion profit in the six months to the end of September, Ialpa argued that Ryanair should “look to executive remuneration and shareholder distributions” for savings.

“Despite Michael O’Leary’s unhelpful intervention, Ialpa will continue to engage constructively with Ryanair management,” it said.

Ialpa is determined to negotiate terms that properly compensate pilots for their contribution to Ryanair’s financial success, its statement stressed.

Rising air fares are unlikely to compensate completely for the airline’s higher fuel bill, so it is seeking savings across its business.

It has slowed pilot and cabin crew recruitment as it will take delivery of just 15 new aircraft next year, according to O’Leary. He noted that few of its existing pilots were leaving.

The company has cut capacity for the winter months, so it will carry 214 million passengers in this financial year instead of the predicted 215 million.

Ryanair is hiring fewer middle managers and has reined in a graduate programme as artificial intelligence enables existing management to “do more with less”, he said.

The company is looking at more ways of using this technology to boost productivity.

It continues to scrutinise airport charges and taxes, moving aircraft to gateways and jurisdictions that reduce these costs, O’Leary said.

Fares have begun rising since the end of September. Ryanair estimates that air fares could increase by more than 10 per cent next year.

But O’Leary said this could approach 20 per cent if the crisis forces vulnerable carriers such as Wizz or Norwegian out of business.

The resulting loss of seats, added to cuts implemented by legacy airlines, would force ticket prices even higher, he said.

]]>Kinga Krzeminska<![CDATA[Apple forecasts margin drop in holiday quarter as rising memory costs bite]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/03/apple-forecasts-margin-drop-in-holiday-quarter-as-rising-memory-costs-bite/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/03/apple-forecasts-margin-drop-in-holiday-quarter-as-rising-memory-costs-bite/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:14:53 +0000Apple warned on Monday that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring gross margin for the crucial holiday quarter, but said it had taken steps ‌to lock in supplies.

]]>David Fouts<![CDATA[Oil steadies after Monday’s 8% dip]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/03/oil-steadies-after-mondays-8-dip/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/03/oil-steadies-after-mondays-8-dip/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:06:32 +0000Brent oil steadied after plunging almost 8 per cent in the previous session, with the US and Iran signalling a willingness to pursue peace talks as the war in the Middle East enters its ninth month.

The global benchmark was near $105 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was below $97 after its biggest decline in three months on Monday. Iran’s president said his government had been granted more authority by the nation’s supreme leader to negotiate, while US president Donald Trump hinted at progress in talks. Still, simmering hostilities are keeping the market on edge.

The US attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, part of a weeks-long campaign of smaller-scale strikes, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing American officials. State-run Islamic Republic News Agency reported five explosions on the island.

“It doesn’t make a lot of sense given how high tension levels are to see price drops” like Monday’s, said Karen Young, senior research scholar in the faculty of International and Public Affairs at Columbia University. “But the news cycle is generating movement, and that will mean it has further to spike if we get to more active US-Israeli kinetic attacks on Iran.”

Monday’s slide came just before American voters head to the polls for the midterm elections, with Trump and the Republican Party facing mounting political pressure over energy prices that have been driven up by the war. The president has repeatedly said he would resolve the conflict one way or the other, while threatening to resume strikes on Iran after the elections.

Trump mouthed “no” when asked by a reporter if attacks on Iran would resume after the midterms. Throughout the conflict, he has frequently threatened new strikes and claimed progress in diplomacy, without substantial breakthroughs. Oil’s slump rippled across energy markets on Monday, with European gas futures falling almost 9 per cent and US heating oil posting its steepest drop in six months.

The plunge on Monday came after global benchmark Brent rallied almost 14 per cent in October, hitting a six-month high, on concerns about renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, despite a revival in exports from the Persian Gulf.

Still, the scope for a diplomatic breakthrough is unclear. Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian did not specify the extent of the authority granted by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei or whether it signals a broader shift in the country’s red lines in indirect negotiations with the US. His remarks were cited by IRNA.

Major differences between the two sides remain. Tehran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted, sanctions eased and frozen assets released before fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime shipping. Washington is demanding concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme. - Bloomberg

]]>Jacquelyn Martin<![CDATA[How graduates can turn AI to their advantage in a job hunt]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/education/2026/11/03/how-graduates-can-turn-ai-to-their-advantage-in-a-job-hunt/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/education/2026/11/03/how-graduates-can-turn-ai-to-their-advantage-in-a-job-hunt/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:01:00 +0000For many recent graduates around the country, while the past few months may have been filled with music festivals, travelling or working hard to save money, it was also filled with hours spent on Indeed and LinkedIn, fine-tuning CVs and writing countless cover letters.

Applying for jobs can feel like a job in itself, and coupled with widespread media coverage of how AI is impacting the job market, it can feel like the system is working against you.

Angela Curran, guidance counsellor and founder of mycareerverse.ie, has seen first hand the inner-conflict that graduates can have towards AI. “They’re at such a vulnerable stage, because they can’t get their foot in the door, and they’re up against AI just to get in the door. Then it becomes a negative connotation to them. They’re frustrated. That frustration is real.”

She notes that graduates are engaging with AI on both sides of the hiring process: employers are using AI to select candidates for interviews, while applicants are increasingly using AI to generate CVs or cover letters. “There’s very little human contact at the first stage in their career plan,” she says.

The signs are AI prefers AI-written CVs, and one law firm’s experience is revealing

She points to the fact that some graduates are now being asked to complete interviews with an AI avatar before being granted an in-person interview.

While it’s certainly true that these factors pose a challenge to graduates, “it’s not all doom and gloom”, Curran says. “AI is there. You have to use it to your advantage.”

Rather than avoiding AI at all costs, Curran says those who take the time to understand how the technology works, and what it means within their sector, will stand out as applicants. “It definitely comes up as an interview question,” she says. “You don’t have to be an expert in it, you just have to know how it works. You have to be able to speak about it.”

She says employers are looking for someone who can “think and adapt and work alongside these machines, not competing against them”.

For those who want to learn more about AI systems, she says there are plenty of courses online that can help them to upskill, giving LinkedIn Learning and Coursera as examples. She reminds graduates that they also should be demonstrating their knowledge of AI to employers, such as through posting the completion of these courses on their LinkedIn page. “On LinkedIn, once you get a certificate, blast it up. As much as you might think that’s cringe ... you’re going to have to put on LinkedIn that you got this certificate, and then people start to notice it. It’s like a marketing strategy.”

From working with graduates, Curran has observed that one place where they can go wrong on the job hunt is over-relying on AI to complete their applications. Many employers now use Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), which can scan and extract text from your CV to categorise your experience and skills.

The system matches your application against the requirements listed in the job description, allowing recruiters to filter candidates who best fit the requirements of the job. This has led to many graduates using AI to curate a CV that mirrors the language of job vacancies they are applying for.

“I see on the ground that students are using AI tools to develop CVs, based on the job interview. They’re asking AI to produce an actual CV based on the job application, and they’re firing that in. They’re not actually using it to build a framework and then put their own information in and populate what they’ve done.”

Rather than completing generic CVs based on job descriptions, she recommends that graduates build off these templates, and consider how their skills match the role they’re applying for. She also reminds graduates to avoid typing all of their personal details into AI.

She says most recruiters can tell quite easily if a CV has been fully generated by AI. “You can see the poor formatting on them, and the language is so Americanised. So people know if they’re written by AI.”

Employers increasingly concerned about job candidates using AI to write CVs

Another place where she sees graduates fall down is applying to too many roles with these AI-generated CVs. “They’re firing off these CVs to everybody and anybody for selection,” she says. Graduates need to ask themselves “what kind of company do you want to work in?”

Curran recommends writing down all the companies you’re applying for in a journal, and reflecting on whether these are places you really want to work.

Graduates should have a “story bank” prepared for applications and interviews, which allows them to not only identify the relevant skills and expertise they have, but demonstrate where they picked up this experience.

Today’s graduates should have “emotional intelligence, critical thinking, all the things that a human person can only do”, she says. Employers want graduates who “realise that the information that we’re getting [from AI] is biased, that AI does hallucinate and gives you an answer regardless of what you think.”

Curran says that AI “amplifies good thinking”, but “doesn’t replace it”.

If you’re still failing to get past the application stage of a role, she says you should try to identify the gaps between the skills required for the role and the ones you possess. “Look at LinkedIn. Look at who’s working in the organisation: what skills have they got? What additional courses did they do?”

She also points to Springboard+ courses as a way for graduates to upskill, a government initiative that offers free and subsidised courses at certificate, degree and master’s level in areas such as engineering, green skills and ICT (information and communications technology).

For graduates considering applying for jobs outside of Ireland, she says AI can be a “great research tool”.

“This is now a global market to play with. It’s not just Ireland,” she says. “AI is helping me with graduates to look beyond Ireland. There’s a huge amount of employment elsewhere. I can pull up all the information around European job listings. I can look into different companies on a European level. The likes of the EU are recruiting huge amounts of graduates at the moment.”

Graduate job coaches offering access to the ‘unwritten rules’ of recruitment

Another way graduates can utilise AI on their side is to use it to practise for job interviews. Curran says applicants can use tools that allow them to practice talking with an AI chat bot ahead of their interview. Listening back to yourself will allow you to improve “how you present yourself and, better your communication skills”, she says.

Finally, Curran reminds graduates that while it may feel like there’s only one way to complete job applications in an era of AI, traditional methods have not gone away.

“That whole idea of knowing someone in a place hasn’t gone completely,” she says.

Using online networks such as LinkedIn to see if you know someone working in a company, or chatting to friends and family members to see if their workplaces have openings is another way graduates can get a foot in the door.

“Start at smaller employers, local employers. Walk with your feet, print your CV out. I’ve seen graduates being really successful with that.”

]]>nicoletaionescu<![CDATA[State requires large number of workers from outside European Economic Area, according to ESRI ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/03/state-still-needs-large-numbers-of-workers-from-outside-european-economic-area/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/03/state-still-needs-large-numbers-of-workers-from-outside-european-economic-area/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Ireland continues to require large numbers of workers from non-European Economic Area (EAA) countries to address labour shortages, but it struggles to retain many of them, according to Economic and Social Research Institute research.

Its report found the number of non-EEA workers – those from outside the EU, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein – that were recruited increased substantially between 2021 and 2025 in all but one of 25 sectors.

The exception was the information and communications technology (ICT) sector, where the number fell 21 per cent, the report to be published on Tuesday said.

Despite the continuing need to recruit high-skilled worked in other areas, especially healthcare, the number of General Employment Permits (GEPs) issued to lower or mid-skill level workers had exceeded, in 2024, the number of Critical Skills Permits (CSPs) going to those with the most urgently needed qualifications or experience. This was the first time this had happened in almost a decade.

The number of CSP holders leaving again after coming to Ireland to work is also substantially higher than those with GEPs with 40 per cent versus 21 per cent after two years and 60 per cent versus 50 per cent after five years.

Citing Department of Justice figures, the research suggests the figures for those with graduate-level education are significantly lower.

The growth in the number of permits issued between 2021 and 2025 was skewed by the Covid pandemic with many migrant workers leaving during that time and many coming here to fill vacancies as workplaces opened up again in its aftermath.

There have also been a number of changes to the regulations during the period with the easing of restrictions on what roles overseas workers could be granted a GEP to fill and, more recently, a review of the circumstances in which the 50:50 rule might be waived. This rule requires that a majority of workers in a workplace be EEA citizens.

The number of companies recruiting from outside the EEA, meanwhile, has steadily grown to 8,328 in 2025. Just 20 of those firms accounted for about 10 per cent of the total of more than 31,000 permits. Google topped a list that included other tech firms as well as some operating in the professional services and health sectors.

However, the majority – 4,740 – only applied for one permit to fill a vacancy.

The number of non-EEA students entitled to work some hours in Ireland to help support themselves topped 56,000, almost double the figure for 2021, with Brazilians making up more than a quarter of the total on 15,077.

“The strong uptake in employment permits shows the growing importance of non-EEA migrant workers in meeting Ireland’s demand for labour across healthcare, construction and ICT services,” said Ada Sophia Hahn, who wrote the report with Dervla Potter.

“Ensuring that the employment permit system is effective and fair matters not only to employers and migrant workers but also to Irish society at large as it could impact the delivery of public services.

“Consistently low retention services would be a concern, as it could undermine the effectiveness of the system.”

Members of the migrant worker community are due to protest outside the Dáil on Tuesday over proposed changes to Ireland’s citizenship requirements.

]]>Robert Kirk<![CDATA[Consumers ‘just about coping’ with financial pressures, credit union survey says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/consumers-just-about-coping-with-financial-pressures-credit-union-survey-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/consumers-just-about-coping-with-financial-pressures-credit-union-survey-says/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Irish consumers feel as though they are “just about coping” with financial pressures, prompted by “increasingly uncertain and largely negative” perceptions of global economic conditions, the Irish League of Credit Unions (ILCU) has said.

They are, however, “a little less glum” than their UK, US and European counterparts, whose individual economic outlook has hit near-record lows caused by “an extraordinary collapse” in consumer confidence.

The ILCU recorded a result of 61.6 on its monthly consumer sentiment index survey – “marginally above” its 59.6 average since March, when war on Iran began to affect the global economy. This is “materially below” the index’s 30-year average of 83, ILCU said.

Media attention on Budget 2027 and the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s criticisms of its spending levels “may have coloured consumer thinking” on the State’s economic outlook as much as the impact of artificial intelligence on economic activity and employment may have had, it said.

David Malone, ILCU chief executive, said the survey’s findings “suggest that sentiment overall remains subdued and consumers continue to be nervous”, with households facing “diverse financial circumstances”.

Consumers expect living costs to rise on average by 3.5 per cent next year, the survey found, only marginally higher than the Economic and Social Research Institute estimate last month that consumer prices would increase by 3.3 per cent in 2027.

Up to four-fifths of respondents indicated they expected a price increase in their household energy bills, while 79 per cent expected the same for grocery costs and 71 per cent for other bills, the survey of 1,000 adults found.

Asked about their own household’s financial situation, 9 per cent described themselves as “very comfortable” while 30 per cent said they were “comfortable” or “managing well”.

Up to 28 per cent of respondents said they were “managing carefully” and 19 per cent were “managing with difficulty”, while a tenth said they were “struggling” and 5 per cent were “falling behind”.

]]>SDI Productions<![CDATA[How can my son find out if his father has cut him out of his will?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000My son’s father and I never married. My ex also has another son who he is very close to. Recently my ex came into some money from the sale of his own father’s house. In the event that he dies, how can our son find out if he left a will?

CC

In an ideal world, we all take care of family, not least when we die, assuming we have the resources to do so. The real world is more messy.

You don’t say whether your former partner was ever a part of your son’s life but he certainly never paid anything to the cost of raising him.

Now middle-aged, your son and his father no longer talk. Meanwhile, his father has a son from a separate relationship to whom he is close, and the father has come into money.

That certainly raises the potential for a dispute when he dies.

There are two scenarios here – one where he has a will and one where he does not. Let’s take them in reverse order.

If there is no will, his estate would be divided according to the Succession Act.

You do not say whether the father ever married – either to the mother of his other son or someone else. If he did, and presuming that spouse survives him, she will receive two-thirds of his estate with his children sharing the final third.

That would include your son, this favoured other son and any other children he might have.

If the spouse does not survive him, or there never was any spouse, the children split the value of the estate between them without regard to favourites. Everything is split evenly.

Whomever applies for the grant of administration intestate is obliged to track down all qualifying beneficiaries – which includes all children regardless of whether they were born inside or outside a marriage. In practice, whomever applies to manage the estate will engage a solicitor as intestacy can be a minefield.

But what if there is a will?

If it is like most other Irish wills and there is a spouse, it will simply leave everything to the spouse. If he does not, the spouse is entitled to what is called a legal right share – which, where there are children, amounts to one-third of the estate.

Assuming any legal right share is respected, the will could make provision for one or other or both sons – and any other children – but it doesn’t have to. There is no obligation for a person to provide in death for adult children or any other relative apart from a spouse.

However, if a child feels that they should be entitled to something in a will, they can take what is called a section 117 action.

Section 117 (1) of the Succession Act 1965 says: “Where, on application by or on behalf of a child of a testator, the court is of opinion that the testator has failed in his moral duty to make proper provision for the child in accordance with his means, whether by his will or otherwise, the court may order that such provision shall be made for the child out of the estate as the court thinks just.”

This is a very wide and nebulous position, with the court taking into account the circumstances of the applicant vis-à-vis other family members among other things.

It clarifies in section 117 (2): “The court shall consider the application from the point of view of a prudent and just parent, taking into account the position of each of the children of the testator and any other circumstances which the court may consider of assistance in arriving at a decision that will be as fair as possible to the child to whom the application relates and to the other children.”

The key thing is that any section 117 application must be made to the court within six months of a grant of probate.

And how do you know probate has been granted? In a harmonious family situation, you’d expect to be notified of this but in the scenario you outline, it may be a case of your son keeping tabs on the Probate Register where all grants of probate and grants on administration (in case of intestacy) are recorded – along with copies of the related will where one exists.

He will need his father’s first and surname and the year in which he died.

When will probate be granted? That depends on how efficiently whoever is managing the estate sort the paperwork and how complex the estate is. It generally takes a year or close to it anyway.

Is it worth pursuing a section 117? That depends on your son’s position in life and also what his father’s estate comprises. There is certainly no guarantee of success and there will be legal fees to consider.

Of course, there is nothing to say that this money your ex has recently come into will still be part of his estate when he dies. It could well have been dissipated by then – either because it was spent or because it was gifted to other family members.

The Section 117 procedure only refers to provision in a will or lack thereof. It does not cover lifetime gifts.

As usual, much of the campaign coverage has revolved around opinion polls, which give the Democrats a national lead of up to 11 points on the generic congressional ballot, while the party’s candidates are challenging for Senate seats in places where they usually wouldn’t have a hope.

Despite all that polling data, many remain sceptical about whether these predictions will be proved correct. Regardless, polls have been central to the coverage, as they are in most elections.

Polling has been a fixture of political journalism for almost 90 years. Its modern form dates from 1936, when George Gallup used a small but carefully chosen sample to predict Franklin Roosevelt’s landslide, humiliating the Literary Digest, whose vast survey of its own affluent readers had backed his opponent. Gallup’s results were syndicated to newspapers across the country, beginning a partnership between pollsters and the press that has lasted ever since.

But it was not until the 1970s, or in Ireland’s case the 1980s, that newspapers began to invest seriously in polls of their own. The Market Research Bureau of Ireland, founded by Jack Jones in 1962, spent years researching washing powder and air travel before turning to politics, and the Irish Times/MRBI series that began in the early 1980s became the benchmark here.

There has been no shortage of criticism of the relationship. Newspapers, it is suggested, over-dramatise results, splashing shouty headlines about tiny shifts that are within the margin of error. Polling is also blamed for “horse race” coverage that treats elections as sporting fixtures, ignoring the issues at stake. One Harvard study of the 2016 US presidential race found policy accounted for just a tenth of coverage, less than a quarter of the space devoted to who was ahead.

These criticisms are not without foundation, although research across 27 European countries suggests poll-driven coverage is most common in tight, multiparty contests, where knowing the state of play can help voters decide how to use their ballots.

Distrust of the polls themselves has also grown, with people pointing to glaring misses such as Brexit or Donald Trump’s first victory. That has been compounded by the rise of populist movements whose supporters are often underrepresented in surveys, prompting accusations of bias. Despite all this, a study of more than 200 elections in 32 countries found no evidence that polling errors were increasing.

Three elections in the past 10 days have highlighted some of these issues. In Brazil, the final surveys had incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead in the first round, which his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro edged, then gave Bolsonaro a narrow lead in the runoff, which Lula won by more than three points. Neither error was particularly large, but each picked the wrong winner.

In Israel, the final polls correctly predicted deadlock but underestimated both Likud and the Arab parties.

And in Serbia, where public polling is sparse and voters had reason to be wary of declaring opposition sympathies, surveys showing Aleksandar Vucic’s party narrowly ahead were proved completely wrong when the student-led opposition won an outright majority.

The Irish Times view on Serbia’s election: youthquake in Belgrade

Traditional polling is being reshaped by changes in the media industry. Falling revenues have made publishers less enthusiastic about the expensive business of high-quality polling. That has led to a move from face-to-face interviewing towards cheaper online panels, weighted to reflect the profile of the electorate.

In Ireland, Red C for the Business Post and Ireland Thinks for the Sunday Independent now alternate monthly online surveys, while The Irish Times’s face-to-face poll with Ipsos B&A appears several times a year. The methods can return somewhat different results. Red C, for example, regularly puts Fianna Fáil a few points lower than other pollsters do. But overall performance has been respectable, with final polls in 2024 largely within the margin of error. Every poll is a snapshot in time, and across volatile referendum campaigns, surveys and results have often diverged wildly.

The field has narrowed too, with titles such as the Sunday Times Irish edition no longer commissioning polls.

Elsewhere, there are signs of questionable standards. In September, an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and the Verbatim group revealed that polls carried prominently by the Times and the Telegraph had been arranged by Reform UK figures and paid for through what they believed was an American donor’s company, without either paper being told.

In the US, a firm called Wedgewood Polls admitted last week that it had fabricated results reported by The New York Times, Newsweek and others. One Michigan Democratic candidate says a fake survey showing her in single digits drove away her donors and ended her Senate campaign.

The problem in both cases lay with news organisations failing to verify where the numbers came from and what financial incentives might have been involved. But what is even worse is that some US outlets are giving prominence to the almost completely unregulated prediction markets that have mushroomed in recent years. CNN and CNBC have partnerships with Kalshi, and Wall Street Journal owner Dow Jones with Polymarket, on undisclosed terms.

This seems a highly dubious proposition, since betting odds can be moved by anyone with deep enough pockets. The old model, in which media organisations paid for polls and stood over the results, may have had its flaws but this particular replacement looks considerably worse.

]]><![CDATA[Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Retirement savers have just another two weeks or so until the November 18th deadline for tax relief on additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) for 2025 passes.

Often described as “turbo fuel” for your pension, the benefits of these payments are many. You can maximise available tax relief, improve your chances of retiring early, and you’ll hopefully have a bigger fund to draw down in retirement thanks to them.

But before you lock your money away through AVCs, it’s also worth taking a moment to consider if they are the best option for your money at a particular point in time.

Your money is locked away

Once you put additional money into your pension, it is locked away until you can retire. But what if you need it for your health? Your children? To pay down expensive debts? Repairs on your house, or just for those holidays you want to take now, rather than wait until retirement?

“It’s really a case of having a financial plan – and prioritising what’s most important,” says Mark Ryan, director of My Wealth Management.

Putting money into the stock market, an investment fund, or a high-yielding deposit account can still give you the potential for real gains, while maintaining flexibility. Of course, you are giving up on the tax relief – but this might be okay.

“Tax relief, while it’s great, shouldn’t be the only consideration. It’s of little benefit if it leaves you short of money for other needs,” says Sinead McEvoy, head of retirement solutions at Standard Life.

For McEvoy, a solid approach can be doing “a bit of both”. Put some money into a rainy-day fund, for example, and some into an AVC.

She is often asked whether or not you should prioritise your pension, or paying your mortgage.

Managing your money and your time in retirement

For some, the psychological impact of paying off a mortgage is huge, and this can take priority when it comes to spare cash. But focusing on it solely may not be the right approach either.

“I don’t think I’d pay off all your mortgage and ignore your pension,” she says. “Think of all the compounding you’re missing out on by paying off your mortgage.”

“It would be a preference for some people,” Ryan agrees, referring to paying down the mortgage first. Another option, he suggests, is to boost your AVCs now, and hope for investment growth, and use the bigger lump sum when you retire to pay down the mortgage at that point.

You won’t benefit from the same tax relief as AVCs by paying down your mortgage, so it can be worthwhile to “crunch the numbers” before making a decision.

Indeed, there can be an opportunity cost of this approach; you are giving up on tax relief, which can supercharge your pension fund.

Consider €200 invested every month for 10 years. If it returns an average of 6 per cent a year, it will deliver almost €32,500. But if tax relief had been available, at the higher rate, you would have had €280 going into the investment each month – so the return would have been significantly higher, at €45,500. You just wouldn’t have been able to withdraw it.

You may end up paying a higher tax rate in retirement

“I get asked this question often,” says Ryan. “Why would I put in money to get tax relief at 40 per cent when I pay it at the same rate in retirement?”

Remember, the tax relief you enjoy on AVCs is only deferred; when you draw down your pension, you may pay income tax on it. So then, you need to bear in mind the value of this tax relief – while it will grow tax-free, which is very beneficial, it can be particularly valuable if you get relief on it today as a higher rate taxpayer, and draw it down at the standard rate of tax in retirement.

While a higher tax rate in retirement is indicative of a healthy fund, it may be a consideration for those close to the higher tax bracket.

“Those on the borderline (of the higher rate), and considering AVCs, then it’s a conversation worth having,” says Ryan. “I have had scenarios where people have decided not to do AVCs because of that.”

Others, however, will opt for the ‘bird in the hand’ approach, and take what’s on offer now – tax relief – rather than predict how the future might play out.

This decision may be only for a certain cohort, however. First of all, to maximise your tax-free lump sum on retirement of €200,000, you will need a fund of €800,000 – 25 per cent is tax-free; amounts between €200,000 and €500,000 are taxed at 20 per cent. “And that’s a significant pension fund for most,” says McEvoy. “Typically, people are underfunding their pensions.”

Lessons for a happy retirement from a year interviewing Ireland’s top leaders

So, paying in AVCs can help bump up your tax-free lump sum.

And, paying tax at the higher rate on your pension “just isn’t the case for most people” says McEvoy, pointing to the more generous tax bands available for the over-65s.

As our table shows, a married couple with an annual pension income of €36,126 won’t pay any tax in retirement, while single people aged 65 and over won’t pay tax on earnings of less than €18,000.

However, as income rises, retirees will see a growing proportion of their income taxed at the higher rate. A single person earning €45,563 from a combination of state pension and private pension income, for example, will pay a certain portion of their income at the higher rate of 40 per cent (€1,563 for 2026), thus pushing their effective rate up to 12.3 per cent. And it increases from there; someone earning €75,563 a year in retirement will pay the top rate of tax on €31, 563 of their income – for an effective tax rate of 24.5 per cent.

AVCs have to be drawn down at the same time as an occupational pension

Having different pension vehicles in play may give you greater flexibility as to when you have to draw down your pension. PRSAs (Personal Retirement Savings Accounts), for example, can be drawn down between 60 – or 50 if it isn’t tied to an employment – and 75. It might also help keep your pension income in retirement taxed at the lower rate.

Remember, however AVCs are funded – either through the main scheme or an AVC PRSA – they are tied to this main scheme.

“When you have an AVC, it must be retired at the same time as the main scheme,” says McEvoy. So, there is no flexibility available when putting your AVC money into a separate pension vehicle.

However, there might be the opportunity to segment your pension into different PRSAs at retirement, so that you can draw them down at different ages.

There is some flexibility, however, if you’re not happy with the fund choices offered in your occupational/public sector scheme.

AVC PRSAs can be used to offer greater investment choice. But the charges might be higher than in your occupational scheme, so this should be considered.

What are AVCs?

In short, AVCs are additional payments you make to your occupational or public sector pension to boost your fund, and hopefully your income in retirement.

If you have already maximised your matching contributions (ie, your employer contributes 6 per cent of salary if you contribute 6 per cent), and you have extra cash, you can consider putting this into your pension via an AVC.

As with all pension savings, the big advantage here is the tax relief you get – if you’re a higher rate taxpayer, for example, a €1,000 contribution to your pension will only cost you €600.

How much you can contribute and avail of tax relief will depend on Revenue limits. Tax relief is offered as a percentage of your net earnings, and increases in line with your age. So, if you’re aged between 30 and 39, for example, you can put 20 per cent of your earnings into your pension and get tax relief on it (so up to €10,000 a year if you earn €50,000, for example). This percentage increases to 30 per cent for those aged 50-54; 35 per cent for 55-59; and 40 per cent for 60 and over.

When it comes to making an AVC, you can do so on a regular or one-off basis, so they offer good flexibility. A maximum annual limit of €115,000 applies.

If you haven’t made AVCs for 2025, and you do so before the online tax return deadline of November 18th, you will be due a tax saving.

Consumers will be expected to pay the charges in one of two ways.

In such circumstances, both charges will be shown to the consumer and the total price paid at the checkout will be the final price, with no extra charges on delivery.

Other websites may not collect these charges at checkout and the delivery company will be required to collect the money from the consumer.

When charges have to be collected in this way it is likely a further administrative fee of about €7 will be added to the total by the delivery company.

The development would require an investment of $350 million to $400 million (€312 million to €360 million), he estimated.

European Union rules require airlines to blend 2 per cent sustainable fuel with the kerosene used to power commercial aircraft. That will increase to 6 per cent in 2030 and to 20 per cent in 2035.

That facility will produce more than 170,000 tonnes of fuel a year, while the partners have confirmed that it will require investment of $400 million. Production is due to begin in September next year.

“Irish airlines have signed up to commitments on sustainable aviation fuel,” O’Connor added.

Irish and global airlines have faced rising fuel bills since the US-Israel attack on Iran in February, which closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas is shipped.

Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary recently warned that this would lead to higher air fares.
