]]>Michael McCarthy<![CDATA[Ireland’s AI moment: making the leap from adopting AI to building it]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/irelands-ai-moment-making-the-leap-from-adopting-ai-to-building-it/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/02/irelands-ai-moment-making-the-leap-from-adopting-ai-to-building-it/Mon, 02 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Ireland has been at the forefront of technology growth in Europe for decades. Many of the world’s largest and leading technology companies have established significant European operations here, creating jobs, investment and expertise and helping Ireland to build a strong, successful technology sector.

AI is the next test of that success. Ireland is already one of Europe’s leading adopters of AI, but the question now is how we use that position to build AI businesses, to develop intellectual property and to create lasting economic value in Ireland.

This question feels particularly timely after the recent International AI Summit hosted in Dublin as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union, which very much brought the topic into focus.

Ireland has spent decades building an enviable position at the intersection of US technology investment and the European single market. Ambition is everything and Ireland should now aim not only to host, regulate and use AI, but also to become a place where valuable AI products are developed and commercialised.

There is a strong foundation from which to do so. Microsoft’s latest Global AI Diffusion report puts Ireland’s AI user share at 49.9 per cent, the highest in the EU and significantly above the global average of 18.8 per cent. It gives Ireland a strong starting point.

Much of the global debate about AI has focused on the foundations of the technology: energy, chips, data centres and large AI models. Those layers do matter and Ireland already has significant assets in technology infrastructure.

For Ireland, however, the greatest opportunity may lie higher up the value chain in the application layer, the applications that turn AI capability into useful products and services for particular industries.

Where Ireland Can Compete

Ireland already has considerable expertise in sectors where AI could change how complex businesses operate, including technology, financial services, life sciences and healthcare. Businesses here do not need to build the next frontier model to create valuable AI intellectual property. They can combine their knowledge of those industries with increasingly capable AI tools to develop products that their clients will actually use and which can solve real commercial problems.

The investment environment is also encouraging.

Pitchbook data records €947.3 million across 182 Irish AI deals since January 2025, including €256 million across 75 deals so far in 2026. It places Ireland second in Europe for AI venture-capital deal count per capita.

More than $250m invested in Irish artificial intelligence firms over first half of 2026

The challenge is to ensure that this activity translates into businesses, intellectual property, specialist employment and economic value that remain in Ireland. None of this will be straightforward.

Energy and infrastructure pressures cannot be ignored, competition for skilled people is intense and other European countries are pursuing the same investment.

Regulatory complexity can also affect where new products are tested and commercialised. That makes it all the more important that Ireland focuses on areas where its existing strengths give it an advantage, rather than trying to replicate the scale of AI infrastructure being developed elsewhere.

Getting Regulation Right

Regulation is part of that picture. Ireland should not have to choose between having effective regulation or having a competitive AI sector. The backing of the Dublin Declaration on trustworthy, safe and sovereign artificial intelligence by EU member states reflects an important principle: trusted AI and competitiveness should reinforce rather than undermine one another.

The Startup Ireland AI Accelerator Programme and the additional €45 million announced for technology centres by 2030 are welcome signals too. But the test will be whether those commitments on policy, investment and regulation work in practice.

Ireland can capture the AI dividend while mitigating the risks

Businesses developing new AI products need to understand how the rules apply and have the opportunity to engage with regulators at an early stage. Regulators have an important role to play in providing that clarity and helping businesses navigate the regulatory framework as new products are developed. Making that work in practice will require sufficient resources and technical expertise within Ireland’s regulators, as well as effective co-ordination between the AI Office of Ireland, the Data Protection Commission and other relevant authorities.

The proposed AI Regulatory Sandbox could also play an important role if it gives businesses practical access to regulators as they move from testing their new products to bringing them to market.

This is not an argument for lighter regulation. Trust matters, particularly in sectors such as financial services and life sciences, and the importance of maintaining trust while supporting innovation was a recurring theme at the International AI Summit.

Ireland’s opportunity is to show that effective regulation and innovation can work together. Businesses need to understand the rules and be able to engage constructively with regulators as new products are developed. Regulation should protect people properly, while being sufficiently clear and proportionate to support investment and the development of new technologies in Ireland.

Ireland’s position in the AI economy is not accidental. It reflects many years of investment, international business experience and accumulated technology expertise. But we should not assume that those advantages will automatically carry over into AI.

Having secured a place in the global AI ecosystem, the question now is whether Ireland remains principally a location where AI is hosted, regulated and consumed, or whether it becomes one where the next generation of AI businesses and applications is built.

The countries that succeed in capturing those added-value investments will shape the next decade of economic growth. Ireland has every opportunity to be among them.

Marie McGinley is a partner and head of the technology and innovation group at Matheson LLP

Ireland, however, slept, with a highly protected and expensive, inefficient domestic manufacturing sector.

In the 1930s, along with most other countries, we introduced protectionist measures to develop domestic industry. These remained in place into the 1960s when Seán Lemass gradually dismantled the trade barriers in anticipation of EEC entry, which we joined in 1973.

The maintenance of protection after the war had not resulted in successful Irish businesses. The process of moving to free trade proved painful. Much of the existing industry could not compete and shut down in the late 1960s and 1970s. It took time for new firms, many foreign-owned, to establish themselves and to reap the benefits of EU market access. This move to free trade eventually proved hugely beneficial for Ireland; it was just a pity it had not happened 20 years earlier.

This experience has lessons for the EU today. The rise of China as a significant world manufacturing centre benefiting from government subsidies, along with hostile and erratic US policy to its trading partners, has sharply altered the world trade order.

These factors have evoked a misguided EU response, of trying to protect domestic manufacturing through raising barriers to trade and “buy EU” regulations. In the long term, freer trade is the best answer, and can raise living standards for all partners. Even in time, the US may come to realise it.

The EU’s policy response of protecting EU firms needs an exit strategy: a reformed business sector must be able to compete again on the world stage. There is a serious danger that the EU could lock itself into an increasingly inefficient and costly world of its own.

The changed external environment came at a time when EU factories were already under pressure. In 2008-2024 EU manufacturing employment fell by 1.5 million. However, 4.5 million people without a degree lost their jobs, while graduate employment went up by 3 million.

The significant loss of jobs among less qualified workers is having significant political consequences and fuelling the successes of Germany’s AfD and Marine Le Pen’s prospect of becoming French president.

France has been particularly badly hit. Some 800,000 lower-skilled manufacturing jobs have gone, and the rise of 200,000 graduate jobs has not compensated. In Germany the increase of 800,000 graduate jobs has almost counterbalanced the loss of 900,000 jobs among those without a degree.

Faced with a world hostile to free trade, a different approach is needed to produce a vibrant and successful EU manufacturing sector. Policy interventions should aim to help EU manufacturing to transition to a world where it can stand on its own feet.

Temporary protection should only be accorded to sectors that have a realistic chance of being able to sell in a global market within a reasonable time scale. Protecting an EU car industry that in future can only sell on a protected EU market would be a strategic mistake.

China leads in battery production and solar panels, not just because of government support, or its ready access to rare earths. It’s because the Chinese have engaged in successful research in materials science, resulting in big changes in battery and solar panel efficiency. If China were selling shoddy products at low prices, that wouldn’t be a problem for potential competitors.

The EU should not give up its ambition to have a strong manufacturing sector offering good jobs. However, it will need to invest in research and innovation to transform EU manufacturing into a world-class supplier.

The drastic cuts by the US government to funding for pharmaceutical research have opened the opportunity for the EU to move into that gap. That could prove a real winner. Such research is key to global pharmaceutical innovation. At the same time, China is coming up on the outside and is investing in this area of research. To make the breakthrough for Europe and be successful, research and innovation in pharmaceuticals must take place on an EU scale. Fragmented research efforts country by country won’t bring the critical mass needed.

Given the changing profile of today’s and tomorrow’s manufacturing businesses, the EU also needs to invest in upskilling its workforce. New businesses and new sectors will need different skills from the past. The capacity to adapt and possession of readily transferable skills can give European workers a new edge.

I hear music when the cash register rings,” the trader Marty Zweig told Jack Schwager in Market Wizards. Who doesn’t?

Investors are often advised to let their profits run, but banking gains feels good. It may also make us feel clever – even if we’re anything but.

A forthcoming Journal of Finance paper, Disposed to Be Overconfident, suggests profit-taking can distort our memories and judgment.

When judging their stock-picking abilities, ordinary investors rarely bother with overall portfolio returns or comparisons with the market. Instead, the study says, they use a simpler scorecard: how many stocks they sold at a profit versus how many sold at a loss.

By selling winners quickly, holding on to losers, and remembering the former more fondly, investors convince themselves they are better stock-pickers than their overall returns suggest.

The researchers found evidence of how skewed this scorecard can be. Ordinary Dutch investors recalled selling an average of 4.22 stocks at a profit over a year, almost twice the 2.17 recorded in their trading histories.

In a subsequent experiment, traders who were forced to sell winning stocks became more confident of their abilities than those forced to sell losers. And yet, the two groups picked virtually the same number of winning stocks and made almost identical overall profits. Simply realising a profit made people feel more skilful than they really were.

Fake news: why investors keep believing stories they know are false

The researchers link this to the disposition effect, the tendency to sell winners too early while hanging on to losers. The resulting scorecard is flattering, with profits banked and remembered, while losses remain unrealised and out of sight.

However, it can drive a vicious cycle: profit-taking builds overconfidence, which encourages over-trading, which degrades wealth through bad timing and transaction fees.

Our pleasure in hearing the cash register ring is natural. However, the sound of money being banked doesn’t mean we know what we’re doing.

]]><![CDATA[Can you really ‘make your money back’ on UK pension in two years and eight months?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/01/can-you-really-make-your-money-back-on-uk-pension-in-two-years-and-eight-months/Sun, 01 Nov 2026 11:22:44 +0000I’m still confused about a UK pensions article you wrote some time back. The person had 20 years of contributions and it takes 35 years to get a full pension, so a difference of 15 years.

Are you saying that if she now pays Class 3 contributions of £956.80 for the next 15 years (costing her not too far off £15k), she will have that £15k back after drawing the pension for two years and eight months?

R O’N

It all seems a bit fantastic but, in pure maths terms, that is exactly how it works. However, there are a couple of “real world” issues you need to take into account that will skew that simplicity.

We will come to that in a bit, but first let’s crunch the numbers.

Hundreds of thousands of Irish people – possibly millions – have spent time working in the UK at some point in their careers before returning home or moving on elsewhere. The fact that they could be entitled to a weekly UK state pension – currently paid at £241.30 (€288.50) a week – could make a big difference to some of them.

In 2026/27 – the current UK tax year – it will cost you £18.40 a week to buy back Class 3 national insurance contributions to boost your UK pension. That comes to £956.80 (€1,145.50) a year.

Regular readers will be aware that the cheaper Class 2 contributions many paid to buy back up to 18 years over cover recently are no longer available to people paying voluntary national insurance from abroad. So Class 3 is where we are at from now on.

The current full UK state pension is, as I said, £241.30 and each year you buy back will add £6.89 per week – one thirty-fifth of 241.30 – to the pension you eventually receive at today’s prices. That amounts to £358.28 extra in pension over the course of a year.

Pensions: The most important step is simply getting started

To find out how long it will take you to “make back” what you have paid in, you simple divide the £956.80 cost by the extra pension you get on the back of it – £358.28. That gives you a figure of 2.67 per cent, or just a shade over two years and eight months.

For someone buying back 15 years, the same holds true: you are simply multiplying both the contributions and the benefit by a factor of 15 so you are not changing the math.

But now we come to where reality intrudes into the basic math.

The contributions you are paying come from already taxed income. As in Ireland national insurance is a form of tax, with a small “t”. But the money you receive in retirement will likely be liable for income tax and USC in Ireland, assuming you live here.

If you are paying income tax at 20 per cent, the extra pension amount into your hand each year for every additional year’s contribution you make drops to £286.62. On that basis it would take you 3.35 years, three years and about four months, to make back what you paid in.

If you pay tax at 40 per cent, the benefit in your pocket falls to £214.97 a year for each year’s additional contribution. On that basis, you would not be in “profit” on the arrangement until 4.45 years after you draw down the pension – close to 4½ years.

How to navigate and maximise Ireland’s State pension

USC will extend that again but, given the multiple rates, I’m not going into that in detail. Suffice to say that it will extend the “pay back” period slightly.

However, on average, an Irish man can expect to live for 15 years in retirement and a woman almost 19, so it still seems like a good idea.

There are a couple of other issues that clearly affect the precise payback time.

One is that you are dealing with currency risk. There is no way of putting a figure on this but, clearly, the euro/sterling exchange rates when you make the payment and when you eventually draw down the pension will be different. Whether that benefits you or penalises you, only time can tell.

Then you need to remember that both the pension payable and the cost of these Class 3 contributions tend to change each year. For instance, the full UK pension rate will rise to £250.70 a week.

You do also need to bear in mind that the British are once again fiddling with how they work out pension increases – largely because the current “triple lock” is proving expensive in the context of other demands on exchequer funds.

Your pension: how to make up for lost time

As of now, the tiple locks guarantees that the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5 per cent. From April 2030, unless things change again between now and then, the link to earnings is gone – leaving pension increases to rise by 2.5 per cent or the rate of inflation, whichever is higher.

The expectation, certainly in Whitehall, is that this will reduce the scale of annual pension increases.

That all makes it difficult to be absolutely definitive on these things but, given that the UK state pension this woman receives in 15 years time (or whenever she subsequently retires) will be higher than it is today, it will in fact take less than the time given above to recover her outlay.

Of course, that does have to be offset against the “opportunity cost” – what return that money might have delivered if invested other than in buying back UK pension years – but we’re definitely not getting into that here.

There is one other issue that might skew the numbers. The 35-year timeline for people to secure a full UK state pension is based on someone who starts paying national insurance in 2016 when the new system came into force.

Of course, for the majority of Irish – and others – who are considering voluntary contributions, their UK national insurance record will have started earlier, many decades earlier in some cases. Under the old system, as I understand it, people could secure a full basic state pension on the back of 30 years contribution – but those who retired on this pension before 2016 receive a lower weekly payment.

So they really need to get a fix on what their UK pension position is.

According to the UK government website, they will work out your starting (2016) position under the new state pension. You will be entitled to the higher of the amount you would have got under the old system or the amount you would qualify for under the new system if it had been in place when you started making contributions.

This is important because you then know how many years of contributions you need to make on a voluntary basis to qualify for the maximum pension. It might not be as straightforward as “I worked there for 20 years, so I need another 15 years of voluntary contributions”... or it might.

Confusing? Yep, but that’s what happens when a country changes the way it calculates pension rights.

Anyway, to get a definitive answer, you can check your current pension situation with the UK authorities. There is a user-friendly online system but it does require a UK government ID which many who once worked in the UK will not have.

The alternatives are to contract them via a dedicated email form they provide, though they do warn that it is taking some time to reply to emails.

You can also try phoning – at +44 (0)191 2187777 – though regular readers will be aware of my view that confirmation in writing is always a good idea. Or you can write to them at: The Pension Service 11, Mail Handling Site A, Wolverhampton, WV98 1LW, England.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3446407/">
   <title>Weichenstellung für Trump-Präsidentschaft</title>
   <description>Am Dienstag wählen die US-Amerikanerinnen und -Amerikaner einen Großteil des Kongresses – Repräsentantenhaus und Senat – neu. Aktuell halten die Republikaner von Präsident Donald Trump in beiden Kammern die Mehrheit. Während viele Umfragen den Demokraten im Repräsentantenhaus eine klare Mehrheit voraussagen, könnte es im Senat knapp werden. Für Trump wird sich weisen, ob er seine Agenda weiter durchsetzen kann oder in den kommenden zwei Jahren mit starkem Gegenwind rechnen muss.</description>

A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country.

Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”.

Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u

— Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026

Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry.

The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection.

However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years.

Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7

— Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026

Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”.

Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”.

At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha.

 

In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream.

Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively.

However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians.

OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat

— DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024

Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”.

Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”.

“One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case.

Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii?

Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F

— Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026

Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland.

The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support.

However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two.

]]> Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/02/polish-ambassador-to-un-becomes-third-envoy-to-resign-amid-crisis-over-constitutional-court/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 21:31:27 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106302

Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw.

All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS.

Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation.

All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026

On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021.

Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively.

While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK.

Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau.

Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022.

On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS.

Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”.

 

The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court.

It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties.

Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government.

Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own.

The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023.

This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful.

Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law.

"On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court.

He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal.

Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid.

While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to.

]]> Poland launches operation along Russian border in response to reports of planned sabotage https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/02/poland-launches-operation-along-russian-border-in-response-to-reports-of-planned-sabotage/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 14:34:01 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106284

Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days.

The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń.

“Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.”

“We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services.

RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups.

 

In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”.

That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region.

A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential.

W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania…

— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026

On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”.

Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK.

However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”.

The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”.

List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz

— Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026

Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train.

In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning.

In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland.

The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations.

]]> First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/02/first-asian-hornet-nest-in-poland-eliminated-but-experts-warn-more-to-appear-next-year/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:28:14 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106273

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

]]> Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/31/polish-president-in-physical-confrontation-with-judges-amid-power-struggle-at-constitutional-court/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 11:37:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106251

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.

However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.

pic.twitter.com/Gk4bPH1pJU

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026

On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.

At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.

The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.

pic.twitter.com/sni7uvIVke

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026

Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.

Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.

Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.

⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.

Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.

At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.

The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.

Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki.

Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”.

On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki.

@PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute.

Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w…

— Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026

Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted.

On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”.

Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki.

“One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.”

]]> Chaos at Poland’s constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/30/chaos-at-polands-constitutional-court-as-government-backed-judges-seek-to-oust-chief-justice/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:55:24 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106234

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.

In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.

In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.

The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.

The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.

In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia.

In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company.

On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack.

The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.”

 

In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”.

Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania.

Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:30:41 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Private workers to get guaranteed pension income for life in bid to close savings gap https://www.cityam.com/private-workers-to-get-guaranteed-pension-income-for-life-in-bid-to-close-savings-gap/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:08:08 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473961

Private sector workers are set to be given access to guaranteed pension income for life, as the government aims to close the retirement savings gap between the public and private sector. Under new plans set out by pensions minister Torsten Bell on Tuesday, providers will be required to offer workers an annual income as standard [...]]]>

Private sector workers are set to be given access to guaranteed pension income for life, as the government aims to close the retirement savings gap between the public and private sector.

Under new plans set out by pensions minister Torsten Bell on Tuesday, providers will be required to offer workers an annual income as standard in retirement.

The plans, dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, will “resurrect” the option of having an inflation protected pension that provides a secure income for private sector retirees.

Roughly 17m workers who are saving into a default pension will be given the option.

DB guarantee

The move is anticipated to bring retirement savings in the private sector closer to that of the public, where workers typically have a defined benefit (DB) pension.

DB schemes guarantee employees a regular, lifetime income upon retirement calculated by length of employment and salary. This differs to private defined contribution (DC) schemes where a worker’s retirement fund is built entirely from money paid by them, their employer and tax relief.

But over the last 30 years, the vast majority of private DB schemes that once provided an inflation protected income have been shut down.

While the introduction of automatic enrolment in 2012 has boosted saving among private workers, the majority of the UK sector are saving into DC schemes, leaving them without automatic financial security in later life.

“Private sector workers deserve a much better deal when it comes to pensions. They are doing the right thing and saving for retirement, but when they get there too many are left without a genuine pension,” said Bell.

“We are resurrecting proper pensions for private sector workers…and in many cases protection against the rising cost of living. Things public sector workers take for granted.”

Financial knowledge and loss of choice

The plan is also designed to stop savers from having to become “investment experts overnight” as most take control of their pot with little financial knowledge which can cause them to make rushed decisions.

According to the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP), around 46 per cent of first-time pension pot accesses involved a pot being fully withdrawn in the 2025/26 tax years, leaving many facing the risk of entering retirement without sufficient funds or being reliant on the state pension.

But Steve Webb, pensions consultant at LCP and former pensions minister under the Coalition government, warned that pensioners lose the “freedom and choice” of how and where to invest that comes with DB schemes.

“The government is right to say that managing a DC pot in retirement through the ups and downs of markets, and with no idea how long the pot needs to last, is challenging.  But there is a danger that the government’s hostility to pension freedoms will lead them to promote ‘lifetime income’ solutions too heavily,” said Webb.

“Many people will have a good level of secure income… and may prefer the flexibility to take their DC pot in ‘chunks’ as needed, rather than spread thinly through the decades of retirement. It is vital that the focus on retirement income does not destroy ‘freedom and choice’ in pensions which have been popular with savers and given valuable flexibility to hundreds of thousands of people in the last decade.”

More people are feeling a financial strain than at any other time in the last two years, polling has shown, with a rise in mortgage bills set to put household budgets under greater pressure.  New City AM/Freshwater Strategy polling has suggested that half of mortgage holders will come off fixed-rate deals by the end of [...]]]>

More people are feeling a financial strain than at any other time in the last two years, polling has shown, with a rise in mortgage bills set to put household budgets under greater pressure. 

New City AM/Freshwater Strategy polling has suggested that half of mortgage holders will come off fixed-rate deals by the end of 2028, leaving them exposed to a huge jump in their mortgage repayments. 

Figures showed that nearly three in ten (29 per cent) people believed they were not confident they would be able to afford the rise in bills while more than half (53 per cent) expected a large increase in mortgages. 

The fresh set of data precedes an expected interest rate hike by the Bank of England to four per cent this Thursday, its first hike since August 2023. 

The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee had gradually brought interest rates down from a peak of 5.25 per cent in a rate-cutting cycle beginning in 2024, although it could once again tighten monetary policy in response to a spike in energy prices due to the Iran war.

According to the industry body UK Finance, an interest rate hike will impact 2.3m households reaching the end of their fixed-rate deals in 2027, many of which were agreed when interest rates were as low as one per cent. 

Most banking groups expect interest rates to rise on Thursday. 

Mortgages set to put families in ‘troubled’ situation

While some lenders are competing to offer better deals as interest rates rise, economists at a government watchdog believe the effective interest rate on the outstanding stock of mortgages will rise from around four per cent this year to five per cent by 2031. This will come as people “roll off mortgages that were fixed when rates were lower”. 

In July, the Bank of England said it expected around 5m households to see their repayments increase by the end of 2028, a higher projection than it had previously made before the Iran war. 

For the typical owner-occupier who is coming off a fixed rate in the next two years, mortgage repayments are set to be £45 higher than previously anticipated. The Bank could upgrade this difference if it opts to raise interest rates and take a more cautious approach on the path of monetary policy in the future.

A rise in mortgages for millions of families could add to a heap of costs facing families over the next year as inflation continues to edge higher and fuel prices remain elevated. 

City AM/Freshwater Strategy polling showed that financial strain was at the “highest level” since tracking began in early 2025 as two in five voters were either cutting discretionary spending or struggling with paying essential bills. 

About one in 10 respondents said they were “troubled” and were incurring debt in order to pay bills. 

Method note: Freshwater Strategy interviewed n=1,219 eligible voters in the UK, aged 18+ online, between 30 October – 1 November 2026. Margin of Error +/- 2.8%. Data are weighted to be representative of UK voters. Freshwater Strategy are members of the British Polling Council and abide by their rules.

]]> 2473940Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Virgin Media O2 confirms thousands of UK job cuts in £800m cost-cutting drive https://www.cityam.com/virgin-media-o2-confirms-thousands-of-uk-job-cuts-in-800m-cost-cutting-drive/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:03:04 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473963

Virgin Media O2 has confirmed plans to slash thousands of jobs in the UK under a push to cut its cost base by around £800m, as it grapples with firmer competition and “paradoxical” regulation in the fibre market. The telecoms giant said around £300m of the total savings would come from cutting its 16,000-strong workforce [...]]]>

Virgin Media O2 has confirmed plans to slash thousands of jobs in the UK under a push to cut its cost base by around £800m, as it grapples with firmer competition and “paradoxical” regulation in the fibre market.

The telecoms giant said around £300m of the total savings would come from cutting its 16,000-strong workforce in the UK, with aims to reduce its staff costs by around 30 per cent by 2029.

The company has not disclosed how many jobs in total will be lost.

The cuts form part of a wider cost-saving drive as Virgin Media O2 seeks to simplify its management structure and reduce spending on contractors and suppliers.

Erhan Gurses, telecoms analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, estimated that the redundancies could generate around £200m in annual gross personnel savings by 2028, with further reductions in contractor spending potentially increasing that figure.

However, he warned that the savings would do little to resolve the company’s balance-sheet pressures, with net leverage potentially remaining close to 5.5 times earnings in 2028, above its target range of four to five times.

“The scale and timing show the cost-saving push has accelerated notably”, Gurses said.

Revenue falls as broadband market shrinks

The restructuring comes as Virgin Media O2 faces pressure from tighter fibre regulation, competition from cheaper broadband rivals and a shrinking market.

In its third-quarter results, the company said service revenue fell 3.5 per cent in the three months to the end of September, with another 23,300 fixed line customer losses on a net basis. It said this was 9,400 fewer than a year earlier.

Overall underlying earnings fell 2.6 per cent in the third quarter as a 5.4 per cent drop in costs failed to offset the service revenue hit.

In a statement, the company said senior leadership changes were “already underway” as part of plans to reduce its “organisational layers”.

“Given the market conditions we face, the regulatory backdrop in fibre and the technological changes sweeping across all areas of the economy, standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth,” said Lutz Schuler, chief executive Virgin Media O2.

The company said it had no plans to close any of its UK offices, including sites in London, Reading, Leeds, Manchester and Glasgow.

The company added that the decision came against comes against a backdrop of “a tough macro-economic climate, an intensely competitive and shrinking broadband market and a paradoxical regulatory direction in fibre that does not reflect economic reality”.

Virgin Media O2 said it had no plans to close any of its UK offices, which include sites in Paddington in London, Reading, Leeds, Manchester and Glasgow.

Fibre competition adds pressure

Virgin Media O2, jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, has also been reviewing its fibre investment strategy as competition intensifies.

The company is understood to be nearing an agreement to use BT’s Openreach network, potentially allowing it to expand coverage without shouldering the full cost of building new infrastructure.

The talks come despite tensions between the two operators, with Virgin Media O2 recently describing BT’s agreed takeover of TalkTalk as a “stitch-up”.

Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority has provisionally raised concerns over nexfibre’s proposed £2bn acquisition of Netomnia. Nexfibre is backed by Virgin Media O2’s shareholders.

The regulator is expected to issue its final decision in December.

Virgin Media O2 said its restructuring reflected a “tough macro-economic climate, an intensely competitive and shrinking broadband market” and a regulatory approach to fibre that it argued failed to reflect economic realities.

]]> 2473963Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Barclays begins early motor finance payouts as FCA sets ground rules https://www.cityam.com/barclays-begins-early-motor-finance-payouts-as-fca-sets-ground-rules/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:13:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473936

Barclays will begin offering payouts to motor finance consumers ahead of the forthcoming legal battle after the City watchdog introduced its “minimum expectations” for lenders wishing to settle early. The bank said it would make payments using the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) redress scheme methodology and acceptance would be optional. Once a consumer accepts the [...]]]>

Barclays will begin offering payouts to motor finance consumers ahead of the forthcoming legal battle after the City watchdog introduced its “minimum expectations” for lenders wishing to settle early.

The bank said it would make payments using the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) redress scheme methodology and acceptance would be optional. Once a consumer accepts the settlement, they cannot subsequently seek additional compensation.

It comes after the FCA said it would begin to release the names of lenders making payouts before the case heads to the Upper Tribunal in February 2027.

“The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme,” the FCA said.

It added lenders would not be able to claim or imply that the regulator vetted or endorsed their specific cash offer and it must be no less than the maximum redress consumers would have received under the original redress.

Under FCA rules, maximum payouts are calculated per agreement and capped at either a full commission refund or the total financing charges paid, plus statutory interest.

“Lenders have been considering making early settlement offers but have been reluctant to move ahead without a clear signal from the regulator. With that reassurance now in place, we could see a number of lenders break cover and begin offering compensation ahead of the wider scheme,” Harry Charalambous, principal at consultancy Broadstone, said.

FCA’s £9bn redress faces backlash

The watchdog is set to defend its redress scheme against three challenges from the industry and one from advocacy group Consumer Voice.

The FCA published its finalised proposals at the end of March, where lenders were put on the hook for £9.1bn, lower than previously expected, after the number of qualifying agreements was reduced to 12.1m from 14.2m. But fierce backlash across the aisle led to its suspension in July.

The Supreme Court partially overturned a landmark ruling on car finance deals last year, rejecting claims that hidden commissions were automatically unlawful. It found one customer’s undisclosed commission created an “unfair relationship”, leaving the door open for an industry-wide redress scheme by the FCA. 

Volkswagen Financial Services, which has set aside £725m for expected expenses, is among the challengers to the scheme as well as Mercedes-Benz and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance.

Many of the City’s top banks have criticised the scheme but chose not to challenge it in the courts. Lloyds Banking Group – which has set aside £2bn in payouts – said whilst it was “disappointed” it would not challenge the scheme.

Barclays has set aside a total £430m provision bill for compensation through its Barclays Partner Finance arm.

A Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson said: “We recognise that some customers have already faced a considerable wait for an outcome on their motor finance complaints.

“By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude.”

Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:  “Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.  

“Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.”

Losses at Prem Rugby champions Northampton Saints halved last season as the Midlands club enjoyed a surge in turnover. 

The team, who won their second Prem Rugby title in three years in May, cut losses for last season to £932,000, down from £1.83m the year prior.

Results released by Northampton Saints this morning cited a number of one-off events that helped turnover rise from £22.3m to £25.7m.
