]]> OPINION: Healthcare’s pilot culture is holding back HealthTech innovation https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/11/opinion-healthcares-pilot-culture-is-holding-back-healthtech-innovation/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:10:20 +0000 https://www.eu-startups.com/?p=373817 Across Europe, HealthTech companies are developing new technologies that can improve patient care, ease pressure on clinicians and help health services make better use of limited resources. But while these technologies are often successful in getting into hospitals in the pilot phase, many struggle to move beyond that and secure long term adoption. This is […]

The post OPINION: Healthcare’s pilot culture is holding back HealthTech innovation appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Across Europe, HealthTech companies are developing new technologies that can improve patient care, ease pressure on clinicians and help health services make better use of limited resources. But while these technologies are often successful in getting into hospitals in the pilot phase, many struggle to move beyond that and secure long term adoption.

This is not a new problem. Companies working with large public healthcare organisations, like the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) or Ireland’s Health Service Executive (HSE), are familiar with the issues surrounding new technology implementation. These organisations work at a considerable scale with complex responsibilities and obligations around patient safety and public spending. In short, widespread implementation of new technology, no matter how innovative, can often be met with hesitancy. 

And while the caution is understandable, with so many companies unable to get out of the pilot phase, it raises the question of whether processes are designed to welcome innovation or whether they are designed to keep healthcare stuck in its ways. 

The problem with pilot culture

Pilots play an important role in healthcare innovation. They allow clinicians to assess whether a technology works in practice, from how patients respond to identifying changes needed before wider implementation. They are the first step to mass adoption of new technologies, but far too frequently, they are also the last step.

Wider adoption of successful pilots can run into issues on many fronts: Who owns the budget needed to buy the technology? Which team is responsible for implementation? How will the technology work with existing systems? Who provides training and support? 

These are all questions that should be obvious but are often addressed far too late and end up stopping adoption in its tracks.

Another issue is the fact that the clinicians who champion pilots are often the people most willing to experiment; some can even be evangelistic about new technologies. However, their colleagues may not have the same priorities or passions and so a technology that works well in one department can struggle to get buy-in from the key stakeholders across other departments.

Procurement can favour the familiar

Procurement is another point where promising HealthTech companies can encounter difficulties.

Healthcare procurement carries the huge responsibility of spending public money, meaning they need to find suppliers that are financially sound with products that must meet the appropriate clinical, technical, and regulatory requirements. They need to have complete confidence in what they’re choosing.

A young, unestablished HealthTech company may not garner that confidence, no matter how effective the solution they have developed is. Young companies are also up against it when it comes to meeting the requirements set out by procurement, which are often designed around suppliers with years of experience securing public-sector contracts.

This creates a difficult cycle where a company needs a contract to build its track record, but needs a track record to secure the contract.

Not to mention the fact that procurement’s decisions can often focus mainly on price, so a technology that carries a high immediate cost may struggle to secure approval.

The result of these issues can be an unintended preference for established suppliers, even when a smaller company has a better approach to a clinical problem.

When caution becomes culture

Similar to the case with procurement, healthcare providers have to make sure that what they are offering the public is backed by an incredibly high standard of evidence and accountability. This can create a culture that puts caution ahead of good clinical outcomes and this can actually create risks of its own, as delaying the adoption of useful technology as a result of being overly cautious can have negative consequences for patients, clinicians and public finances not to mention the commercial consequence for Europe.

HealthTech startups need to generate revenue, build a sustainable business and invest in further development. If the route from pilot to procurement remains unpredictable, companies may struggle to plan their growth or attract the investment required to expand. 

For many it may push them to look to markets where purchasing decisions are more straightforward, meaning healthcare organisations risk losing access to innovations developed close to home, while European companies lose opportunities to build global businesses from their early clinical successes.

Build the route to scale from day one

There are practical steps healthcare systems can take to improve the path from pilot to adoption.

First, the people responsible for implementation and procurement should be involved early. An enthusiastic clinician on-side is valuable, but a pilot also needs buy-in from finance, IT, operations, procurement and those who will support the technology after launch. They can’t be overlooked.

Second, pilots should be designed with scale in mind. Before a trial begins, the organisation and supplier should agree what success looks like, which outcomes will be measured and what evidence would justify wider deployment. They should also consider training, integration, support costs and the effect on existing workflows.

Third, procurement requirements should better balance risk, costs and the long-term benefits of proposed technology. And the evidence new healthcare companies are required to give should be proportionate to the contract and the potential consequences of failure. The size and the experience of the company should not determine the outcome if the solution they are offering is genuinely helpful to clinicians and/or patients.

Finally, healthcare organisations should learn from their own pilots. Sharing results, including unsuccessful projects and the reasons behind them, can reduce duplication and help other teams make better decisions when it comes to their own pilots. Working in silos doesn’t help anyone.

Innovation needs a destination

The NHS has previously recognised the importance of tackling the problems with pilot culture through innovation guidelines, which help innovators navigate the routes towards wider use.

In Ireland, the HSE’s Framework for Health Innovation was also introduced this year with the explicit aim of creating a more consistent pathway from local ideas and pilots to lasting impact across the health system.

These initiatives point towards the same underlying need: successful experiments must have a realistic route into everyday healthcare.

Europe has the talent and entrepreneurial ambition to build world-class HealthTech companies. Giving those companies a credible route from evidence to adoption will help ensure their innovations have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference.

]]> SpaceTech company Tumbleweed has raised €6.9 million, allegedly the largest SpaceTech Seed round ever raised in Austria, four months after the startup put the country’s first commercial satellite in orbit.

The round was led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, early backer Prototype Capital, and EWOR. Notably, over one-third of Tumbleweed’s 25-person team also invested personal funds.

“This funding will allow us to scale what we’ve proven on our first mission, Oasis Alpha: that microgravity can be a widely accessible industrial resource. We’re so excited to be able to bring this transformative capability to even more customers, and ultimately build a future where microgravity is used to make 10x better cures for cancer, 10x better semiconductors and 10x faster developed pharmaceuticals,” says Julian Rothenbuchner, Tumbleweed CEO and co-founder.

Tumbleweed’s funding follows a series of European SpaceTech financing announcements in 2026.

In Germany, ATMOS Space Cargo raised €25.7 million to develop orbital transport and re-entry services, while deltaVision secured €10.2 million to expand spacecraft component production.

Elsewhere, UK-based NewOrbit raised €16 million for its very-low-Earth-orbit satellite technology, and Switzerland’s Stellar Alpina secured €3.8 million for in-space propulsion systems.

In Austria, Vienna-based ENPULSION secured €22.5 million in March to expand its spacecraft propulsion business.

Together with Tumbleweed’s newly announced round, these financings amount to approximately €85.1 million.

“The fact that Austrian space technology is mobilising international private capital and is
already being used commercially in space sends an important signal about the strength of our research and business location. Companies like these strengthen domestic value creation, create skilled jobs, and demonstrate that Austria is internationally competitive in demanding future technologies,” adds Peter Hanke, Austrian Federal Minister for Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure.

Founded in 2024, Tumbleweed sells modular payload containers (aka Pods) to labs, manufacturers and R&D teams. Pod is a modular payload container that handles power, data and certification.

The Pods are fault-isolated payload containers that arrive pre-certified and keep customer experiments powered and connected in orbit. Research groups, manufacturers and R&D teams send their payload directly to Tumbleweed, and receive data during flight. Pods come in different sizes, and mission costs start at €15k.

Oasis, their spacecraft, takes the Pods up, operates them, and brings them back to earth.

Compared to equivalent experiments conducted via the International Space Station, Tumbleweed customers reportedly ship 5x faster and 10x cheaper.

“Tumbleweed put Austria’s first commercial satellite in orbit in less time than it usually takes to certify a single experiment. Julian has done exactly what he told us he would do when we first met him, only faster. Now every lab and manufacturer can use space without becoming a space company first,” says Daniel Dippold, CEO of EWOR.

Oasis Alpha was built in nine months, five times faster than industry standard, and launched on 7 July 2026 aboard SpaceX Transporter-17 as Austria’s first commercial satellite, carrying four customers. The mission was sold out a year before launch and paid for upfront.

Today’s funding will fund three missions in 2027, carrying more than 10 customers. The capital will also accelerate development of Oasis Beta, Tumbleweed’s next-generation orbital platform scheduled for 2028, which will support larger payloads and feature re-entry capability to safely bring experimental samples back to Earth.

]]> Berlin-based VC firm Robin Capital has closed its second €15 million fund, bringing total commitments across its two early-stage funds to €30 million.

The new fund, Robin Capital Fund II, follows the firm’s first €15 million vehicle closed in 2024. It has already made 17 investments, including SkySpy.ai, Marble Imaging and Helicity Space, which operate across intelligence, defence, Earth observation and space technology.

Robin Haak, Founder and General Partner at Robin Capital, says: “They call it a Solo GP, but nothing about building Robin Capital has ever been solo. Our limited partners, founders, and venture partners are what make this possible. We believe the best venture capital partnerships are built on trust, conviction, and a genuine willingness to help one another succeed.”

Robin Capital’s latest close joins several European early-stage VC fund announcements in 2026.

In Germany, Munich-based Vanagon Ventures closed a €20 million fund targeting pre-Seed AI and DeepTech startups, while Berlin-based Angel Invest and Auxxo secured €40 million and €33.3 million, respectively.

Elsewhere, Barcelona’s Masia closed €18 million, Monaco’s Monte Carlo Capital reached a €13 million first close for its second DeepTech and SpaceTech fund, and Belgium’s Solo GP-led NewSchool VC closed €10 million.

Together with Nuremberg-based ZOHO.VC‘s €7 million first close, these announcements represent €141.3 million in reported fund capital, rising to €156.3 million including Robin Capital’s new fund.

Robin adds: “We want to build a home for exceptional founders, and stay with them long enough to help build exceptional companies.”

Founded in 2023 by entrepreneur and investor Robin Haak, the firm focuses on pre-Seed and Seed-stage investments in European startups, with a particular interest in AI, enterprise software, robotics, defence, space and DeepTech.

Robin Capital typically invests between €100k and €600k in early-stage companies, primarily across Europe. Rather than following strict sector boundaries, the firm looks for founders addressing large markets with the potential to build scalable businesses.

The firm’s investor base includes entrepreneurs, unicorn founders, technology executives, family offices and investors with experience in venture capital and private equity. Its limited partner community includes entrepreneurs and families associated with businesses such as Ferrari, Moratti, Adyen and FTMO, alongside investors connected to Permira, Macquarie and FJ Labs.

Robin Capital operates under a Solo General Partner (Solo GP) model, with Haak leading investment decisions while drawing on a network of venture partners, limited partners and more than 100 experienced operators.

Its first fund has backed European technology companies including Simsalasim, Uvionix, Paypercut and Xaver. Meanwhile, Fund II is building a portfolio with a stronger emphasis on emerging technologies, particularly applications of AI, autonomous systems and space infrastructure.

Beyond its two early-stage funds, Robin Capital has established three dedicated growth Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) to support ARX Robotics, Almetra and Ground A. These investment vehicles enable its investor community to participate in additional financing opportunities beyond the firm’s typical pre-Seed and Seed-stage investment strategy.

Before establishing Robin Capital in 2023, Haak built a career spanning entrepreneurship, corporate operations and venture capital. In 2013, he co-founded Jobspotting, which subsequently became part of SmartRecruiters, where he served as Global COO and Managing Director. SmartRecruiters was later acquired by SAP.

Earlier in his career, Haak worked in mergers and acquisitions at Axel Springer and co-founded Axel Springer Plug & Play. He also made the first institutional investment in German fintech N26 and subsequently served as a General Partner at European growth investment firm Revaia.

Over the past decade, Haak has invested in more than 60 companies, including seven unicorns, among them N26, Algolia, Aircall and Coralogix.

Looking ahead, Robin Capital plans to establish a third €15 million early-stage fund, with the ambition of managing three such vehicles and backing approximately 80 to 90 startups in total. The firm is also considering a dedicated growth continuity fund as part of its medium-term strategy, which would allow it to continue supporting selected portfolio companies as they scale.

The post Solo VC Robin Capital closes €15 million second fund to back AI, robotics and space startups appeared first on EU-Startups.

The post Is Mistral overlooking Europe? 10 homegrown startups that could join its connector ecosystem appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Of the 12 companies listed by French AI unicorn Mistral as available Connectors (ready-made integrations connecting AI to external applications), not one hails from Europe; raising questions about the continent’s competitiveness.

Despite what this may imply, there are plenty of European software platforms that could potentially become managed Connectors for Mistral – many of which have even seen significant backing over the past five years.

Mistral’s Connectors allow users to link its AI tools with external services such as Gmail, Slack, Notion, GitHub and Stripe. Once connected, users can ask the AI assistant to retrieve information, analyse records and, where authorised, perform actions across those services without navigating between different applications.

Drawing on EU-Startups’ coverage between November 2021 and November 2026, here are 10 European startups and scale-ups whose products could plausibly join Mistral’s managed connector ecosystem.

The European Connectors

Attio (United Kingdom): Founded in London in 2019 by Nicolas Sharp and Alexander Christie, Attio raised €44 million in August 2025. The startup develops an AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) platform that helps businesses organise customer information, manage sales pipelines and automate workflows.

Attio is particularly suited to the connector concept because its software acts as a central repository for customer relationships. Its developer platform already supports a REST API, webhooks and OAuth authentication. A potential Mistral connector could allow sales teams to retrieve customer records, identify outstanding opportunities or update pipeline information through natural-language instructions.

Cloudsmith (United Kingdom): Belfast-based Cloudsmith raised €61.5 million in April 2026 in a Series C round. Founded in 2016 by Alan Carson and Lee Skillen, Cloudsmith provides a platform for managing, distributing and securing software packages and repositories. Its product allows engineering teams to control the software components used across development environments and monitor software supply chains. Unlike companies whose primary offering is integration middleware, Cloudsmith operates a standalone developer platform with its own customer accounts, records and management workflows.

Its REST API could support a future Mistral connector, particularly within Vibe Code. Developers could potentially inspect repositories, retrieve package information or review software supply-chain policies through AI-assisted workflows.

Factorial (Spain): Founded in Barcelona in 2016 by Jordi Romero, Bernat Farrero and Pau Ramon, Factorial raised €129 million in June 2026 in a Series D round. The financing valued the business management platform at €2.1 billion. Initially focused on human resources, Factorial has expanded into areas including expense management, project management and training. Its platform helps companies manage employee information, leave requests, administrative tasks and internal processes.

Factorial also offers an API and OAuth-based integrations. A potential Mistral connector could enable authorised managers to retrieve employee records, check outstanding leave requests or review administrative workflows. Its broad range of business functions makes it a credible candidate for extending Mistral’s capabilities beyond communications and project management.

Mews (Netherlands): Amsterdam-based Mews raised €255 million in January 2026 in a Series D round. Founded in 2012 by Richard Valtr and Matthijs Welle, the company develops a hospitality operating system covering reservations, hotel operations, guest management and payments. Mews also offers an Open API ecosystem, including a Connector API that allows third-party software to access hotel operational data.

While this API is not itself a Mistral-managed connector, it provides a possible route for integration. Hotel operators could potentially ask Mistral to retrieve booking information, examine occupancy records or identify operational tasks requiring attention.

Pennylane (France): Paris-based Pennylane secured €75 million in April 2025. Founded in 2020, with Arthur Waller among its co-founders, the company combines accounting, invoicing, expense management and financial reporting in one platform. Members of its founding team previously worked on PriceMatch, which was acquired by Booking.com in 2015. Pennylane provides APIs for accessing financial information and supports OAuth for integration partners. This makes it a potentially useful connector destination for Mistral, particularly for small and medium-sized businesses.

With appropriate permissions, an assistant could retrieve outstanding invoices, inspect accounting records or prepare summaries of company expenditure. However, because the platform handles sensitive financial information, any managed integration would need appropriate authentication and access controls.

Perk (Spain): Founded in Barcelona in 2015 by Avi Meir, Javier Suarez and Ron Levin, Perk secured €191 million in January 2025 in a Series E round. Rebranded as Perk in 2025, the platform allows companies to organise employee travel, bookings, invoices and spending. Its developer tools include REST APIs, webhooks and access to travel and expense data.

A potential Mistral connector could allow employees to retrieve travel itineraries, review bookings or request expenditure information without opening the travel management platform.

Personio (Germany): Munich-based Personio raised €190 million in June 2022 in an extension of its Series E financing. Founded in 2015 by Hanno Renner, Roman Schumacher, Arseniy Vershinin and Jonas Rieke, the company develops an HR software platform for SMBs. Personio provides tools for employee administration, recruitment, attendance, absences and other people-related workflows. Its developer platform supports third-party integrations through APIs with configurable access to employee and organisational information.

A managed Mistral connector could potentially help HR teams retrieve authorised employee records, inspect absence information or review administrative processes. However, integration design would be particularly important given the sensitivity of HR data and the permissions required to access it.

Spott (Belgium): Leuven-based Spott raised €18.3 million in September 2026 in a Series A round. Founded in 2024 by Lander Degreve, Manu Vanderveeren and Samuel Smeys, the company develops recruitment software combining applicant tracking, CRM and AI-powered workflows. The platform helps agencies organise candidate records, manage vacancies and coordinate recruitment activities. Spott also advertises an open API for custom integrations, alongside its separate MCP offering.

A potential featured Mistral connector could enable recruiters to search candidate databases, review recruitment pipelines or retrieve vacancy information through natural language. Its focus on a specific professional workflow makes it a particularly interesting candidate alongside broader business applications.

Storyblok (Austria): Linz-based Storyblok raised €73.6 million in June 2024 in a Series C round. Founded in 2017 by Dominik Angerer and Alexander Feiglstorfer, who previously worked together at a digital agency, the company offers a headless content management system that allows businesses to create and manage content across websites and digital channels. Storyblok has documented APIs for retrieving, creating and updating content, including OAuth-based access to its Management API.

A managed Mistral connector could potentially allow marketing teams to locate published material, prepare website updates or manage content without manually navigating the platform. This would give Mistral a practical connection to the publishing and content-management workflows used by businesses.

Typeform (Spain): Barcelona-based Typeform secured €123 million in March 2022. Founded in 2013 by Robert Muñoz and David Okuniev, the company develops online forms, surveys and interactive experiences for collecting information. Typeform’s documented APIs and OAuth authentication provide a technical basis for third-party integrations.

If Mistral introduced a managed Typeform connector, users could ask their AI assistant to summarise survey results, identify recurring customer complaints or create forms directly from a conversation. This would give Mistral access to a type of structured feedback data not currently represented by its featured connectors.

]]> Roleo, an Estonian personal AI career agent, has raised €2.9 million to expand across Europe and help tech professionals discover career opportunities – without the hassle of searching and applying.

The round was led by the Baltic venture capital firm Practica Capital and included participation from Nordic VC Inventure. The company has secured €3.46 million in total funding to date.

“Most people spend years building their careers, but only actively manage them when something goes wrong or they decide it is time for a change. Meanwhile, great opportunities come and go, often without the right people ever hearing about them,” says Janer Gorohhov, co-founder and CEO of Roleo.

“We believe everyone should have a personal active career agent that understands what they want, keeps an eye on the market, and brings relevant opportunities to them. You should be able to focus on doing great work without missing out on what could come next.”

Roleo’s funding comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered recruitment and workforce technology in 2026.

In September, London-based Jack & Jill raised €34.68 million for its AI agents connecting jobseekers and employers, while Belgium’s Spott secured €18.3 million for recruitment software.

Other rounds included €6 million for France’s HrFlow.ai, €3.4 million for the UK’s inploi and €1.8 million for Belgium’s Ringtime, alongside €18.09 million for Spain’s Orbio and €5.3 million for Iceland’s 50skills.

Together with Roleo, these eight selected rounds represent approximately €90.5 million in newly announced funding.

Roleo’s lead investor announced the closing of its €80 million Baltic-focused fund in 2024 – which has presumably helped mobilise today’s investment

“We saw potential in the Roleo founders – their proven operational experience and grounded, yet very high ambition. They came with a clear short-term plan and a long-term vision that’s easy to relate to. Leading this round was a natural fit for us, and we believe they are the team best positioned to set a new standard for how people build their careers,” adds Donatas Keras, Partner at Practica Capital.

Founded in 2025, Roleo is a personal AI career agent for technology professionals, designed to help people discover relevant opportunities and manage their careers without constantly having to search for their next job.

The company was founded by Janer Gorohhov, co-founder of identity verification unicorn Veriff, and Vahur Hansen, a former member of Wise’s early engineering team and co-founder of startup Membo.

Roleo learns about each user’s experience, ambitions, and preferences, identifies relevant opportunities across Europe, and connects professionals directly with employers when there is mutual interest – without the candidate submitting a job application.

Unlike traditional job boards, which require candidates to search and apply, Roleo builds an understanding of what each individual wants from their career. This includes not only their skills and previous roles, but also their expectations around compensation, flexibility, responsibilities, and future development. Users remain in control of their visibility, personal information, and whether they wish to pursue a particular opportunity.

Roleo’s user base already includes people from leading technology companies such as Google, Amazon, Stripe and Spotify. The service is free for professionals.

“AI is already changing how people handle everyday tasks, from managing information to organising their finances. Yet career management still requires people to do most of the work themselves,” Janer said.

“We want to build something that stays with you throughout your career, learns what matters to you, and helps you make better decisions over time. The goal isn’t to have AI make career decisions for people, but to make sure they have the right information and opportunities when those decisions matter.”

Since the beginning of 2026, Roleo’s agent has connected its users with 30,000 career opportunities they explored further.

Today’s funding will support both the company’s expansion across European markets and further product development, making Roleo increasingly responsive to individual needs and expanding the ways it can support users beyond job matching.

Markus Villig, angel investor, founder and CEO of Bolt, added: “I’ve watched Janer build Veriff and I know what Vahur did at Wise. Both know first-hand how hard it is to find and hire great people across Europe.”

“Hypersonica is redefining how advanced defence capability gets built. Founded in 2023 with engineering teams spread across its Munich HQ and its wholly-owned subsidiary in London, Hypersonic is building what it describes as a first-of-kind, sovereign and cost-effective hypersonic strike capability, one that operates without ITAR restrictions and is developed entirely within Europe.

Led by co-founders Dr. Philipp Kerth and Dr. Marc Ewenz, the startup set out to address the fundamental challenges of hypersonic flight, where extreme aerodynamic heating renders conventional aerospace technology obsolete at speeds beyond Mach 5. The startup overcomes this challenge with state-of-the-art materials, control architectures and avionics capable of delivering stable and manoeuvrable flight.

Since its €23.3 million Series A in February 2026, Hypersonica has successfully tested its prototype HS-1, achieving speeds above Mach 6 over a range exceeding 300 kilometres, becoming the first privately funded European defence company to reach that milestone. The company says its prototype achieved speeds above Mach 6 at industry-beating cost-effectiveness, claiming its development model reduces costs by more than 80% compared to conventional approaches.

The Series B funding comes as governments across the continent move from debating the need for long-range strike capability to actively funding programmes to shore up their security. The UK’s Defence Investment Plan has announced an initial €921.5 million (£770 million) over four years for the UK-German Deep Precision Strike (DPS) programme under the Trinity House Agreement, while a NATO-led multinational initiative has announced €44.28 million (£37 billion) of investment in DPS capabilities over the coming decade.

“The debate about whether Europe needs hypersonic deep-strike capability is over. Governments have recognised the requirement and begun funding programmes. The challenge now is delivery. Europe needs credible hypersonic long-range capability, and more value for every pound and euro it spends,” said Dr Kerth and Dr Ewenz, co-founders of Hypersonica.

The fresh capital will be used to accelerate the development of its deep-strike systems, increase testing cadence, expand operations and reindustrialisation across Europe. The financing will also create hundreds of highly skilled engineering and manufacturing jobs across the UK and Germany.

Hypersonica aims to have its hypersonic deep-strike systems fully developed by 2029, while simultaneously building a broader European technology and manufacturing base with a goal of production at scale.

]]> Gallium Defense, a Paris-based startup working on drone detection at a fraction of the cost of legacy systems, has emerged from stealth with a €7.1 million Seed funding round.

The round was led by Keen Venture Partners and 360 Capital, with participation from Omnes Capital and Polytechnique Ventures. This announcement coincided with European Defence Week 2026, held from 2nd to 6th November in Paris. 

“Great defence starts with superior visibility. Gallium Defense has the team, the industrial partners and the cost model to make drone detection a standard layer at every critical site – the kind of European capability our fund is proud to back,” said Alexander Ribbink, General Partner, Keen Venture Partners.

Gallium Defense was founded in April 2026 by Eric Fournier, Florian Lemoine, and Robin Mandel, three individuals with defence and industrial backgrounds. Fournier spent 17 years advising defence and aerospace leaders at Boston Consulting Group, while Lemoine has over 15 years’ experience in defence and served as a former adviser to NATO SACT. Mandel also brings over 15 years’ experience across industry and consulting through roles at Thales, BCG and Safran.

The company says more than 80% of critical infrastructure sites and military assets remain exposed to modern drone threats because of lack of affordable, field-ready radars capable of addressing the threat at scale. Gallium Defense was formed to address this gap by making high-performance radars affordable and easier to deploy, for both air security and air defence.

“As drones proliferate, traditional radars are reaching their operational and economic limits. At Gallium Defense, we started from a blank sheet with a simple question, asked by operators in the field: how do you meet 80% of the need at 20% of the price? Our answer: a radically rethought AESA radar architecture that makes extensive use of commercial off-the-shelf components and the power of embedded computing,” said Fournier, CEO and co-founder of Gallium Defense.

Gallium’s flagship product is called the GDS-10, an X-band AESA radar with a software-defined, AI-native architecture. It is designed for dual use and comes in two versions: one for critical infrastructure operators and one for armed forces.

The GDS-10 is capable of detecting Class 1 and FPV drones at a range of 10km. It provides 360° azimuth coverage and 90° elevation coverage with no blind spots, and can track multiple drones simultaneously, including within a swarm, day and night, in all weather conditions. Since GDS-10 is software-defined by design, its capabilities can evolve as new threats emerge.

“Our radars are designed to be manufactured and deployed by the hundreds, not one at a time,” said Mandel, COO and co-founder of Gallium Defense.

Just four months after closing its Seed round, the company conducted its first open-air field trials. The funding is being used to industrialise production of its first products, strengthen the team, train AI models, and run demonstrations for civil and military operators around the world. 

With the Seed funding raised and monthly field demonstrations underway, Gallium Defense is pitching itself as the sovereign European answer for drone detection at scale. The company plans to open orders for the GDS-10 in the first quarter of 2027.

]]> Marble Cognition (Marble), a Munich-based startup building AI coworkers that understand how work is executed to optimise and automate business operations, has raised €3.35 million ($3.75 million) in a pre-Seed round. 

The round was co-led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, with participation from angels including a board member of Datadog, a founder of Personio, and executives from McKinsey, Mistral AI and Lovable. The funding will scale inference, grow the engineering team in Munich, and support a US launch.

Reshma Sohoni, General Partner at Seedcamp, said, “Seedcamp has a long tradition of backing founders who change how we work, from UiPath and Synthesia to Marble today. Most companies want to automate more, but the hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done. Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future. We’re proud to back them from the start.”

Marble Cognition was founded in late 2025 by Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit, who met at Munich’s CDTM programme. The company states that it learns how work actually gets done inside a company, turns it into systems AI can read, and then deploys Marble Coworkers: AI agents that take over manual white-collar work. 

The company highlighted that, in an era when software is becoming a commodity, and so is building AI agents, the real value lies in knowing exactly what to automate. However, it notes that this is difficult, because every company runs on processes nobody has written down.

“McKinsey estimates that today’s technology could, in theory, automate about 57% of US work hours. Yet in almost every company Marble works with, around 90% of core processes live only in inboxes, spreadsheets and the heads of the people doing them. That, not the technology, is the biggest blocker to AI transformation. What is missing is an exact picture of how the work is done,” the German startup mentioned in the press release. 

Marble claims to build that picture. It observes how teams work, turning every process into a structured map that AI can read like code. It then builds Marble Coworkers that run the process end to end in the tools teams already use, with humans in the loop where judgement matters. 

It argues that traditional automation bends a standard product to fit a company’s processes. Marble states that it productises the understanding of the process itself.

Explaining its privacy and security measures, Marble says it anonymises everything it captures before any person or AI model sees it, even in the customer’s own cloud. Marble’s desktop app records screen activity, clicks, and keystrokes in the business apps people use at work, never private apps, private tabs, or anything outside working hours. It further notes that employees can pause it at any time, and data is only analysed in aggregate, not based on individuals.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work. But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the way your best people do,” said Rösner. 

Notable customers include EGYM, Mutares and Enam, alongside other tech unicorns, PE-backed organisations and AI roll-ups backed by top-tier funds.

The company reported that at a PE-owned US financial services company, a Marble coworker slashed handling time per case by 90%. In the first month, the team handled 50% more cases without hiring anyone new. The coworker prepares every settlement offer for a specialist to approve. Marble learned the process by watching the team, not from documentation.

In a statement, the authority expressed “deep sorrow” over the accident involving the two helicopters during landing in the Pheriche area.

Video footage circulating on social media appears to show the helicopters approaching the landing area before their main rotor blades make contact. The footage captures the aircraft in close proximity immediately before the collision.

The cause of the accident has not been established.

Fishtail Air initially reported that passengers and crew members had been rescued and were being transported to capital Kathmandu.

In a subsequent statement, the operator confirmed the death of Balaramudu, who had been travelling aboard its helicopter.

Both helicopters belong to the Airbus AS350 family, a widely used series of single-engine aircraft designed for passenger transport, aerial work and operations in demanding environments.

Air Dynasty identifies its helicopter, 9N-AOD, as an AS350B3e powered by a Safran Arriel 2D engine.

According to the operator’s published fleet specifications, the aircraft has a maximum take-off weight of 2,250 kg and a stated maximum operating altitude of 23,000 feet.

The AS350B3e, marketed today as the Airbus H125, is known for its high-altitude performance and is widely used in mountainous regions.

Fishtail Air identified its aircraft, 9N-AJR, as an AS350 helicopter in its accident statement.

Pheriche lies at approximately 4,200 metres above sea level in Nepal’s Khumbu region, surrounded by steep Himalayan terrain and close to the trekking route towards Everest Base Camp.

Helicopters are an essential means of transport in the area, particularly where road access is limited or unavailable. They carry tourists and mountaineers, deliver supplies and undertake medical evacuations.

Flying at such elevations requires careful management of aircraft performance because thinner air reduces the lift available from helicopter rotors and affects engine performance.

Mountain weather and confined landing areas can present additional operational challenges. However, investigators have not indicated whether any of these factors contributed to Tuesday’s collision.

The aviation authority has not announced a timetable for completing its investigation.

]]>
In Brief 8 min read
  • NASA’s Swift telescope faces fiery re-entry after 22 years transforming gamma-ray burst astronomy.
  • Swift observed 2,000+ cosmic explosions, black holes and supernovae before mission end.
  • Failed robotic rescue leaves NASA observatory heading for uncontrolled Earth re-entry.

A NASA space telescope that spent nearly 22 years chasing some of the most powerful explosions in the universe is now heading towards Earth, with its final journey expected to end in a fiery plunge through the atmosphere within days.

The 1.5-tonne Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, launched in November 2004, is expected to make an uncontrolled re-entry around Friday, 6 November, according to satellite trackers. NASA has not confirmed an exact date or location.

Most of the spacecraft is expected to burn up as it encounters the atmosphere, although some of its heavier components could survive and reach the surface. The likelihood of debris causing injury is considered low.

It is an unusual ending for a spacecraft that was still making scientific observations just weeks ago.
Swift was designed to operate for two years. Instead, it spent more than two decades studying exploding stars, black holes and mysterious flashes of radiation from distant galaxies. Its observations helped scientists understand events that take place billions of light-years away.

NASA formally ended the mission on 20 October after the spacecraft descended to an altitude of about 275 kilometres, where increasing atmospheric drag made it impossible to keep its telescopes steadily pointed at astronomical targets.

The spacecraft’s final descent follows an unsuccessful attempt to save it using a privately developed robotic servicing vehicle.

A telescope that could turn towards an explosion in a minute

Swift was unlike many traditional space telescopes.

Rather than spending hours examining a particular patch of sky, it was built to respond quickly when something extraordinary happened elsewhere in the universe.

Its principal targets were gamma-ray bursts, enormous releases of energy associated with some of the most violent events in space.

Some occur when massive stars collapse and form black holes. Others are associated with collisions between neutron stars, the extraordinarily dense remains of dead stars.

These bursts can release tremendous amounts of energy in seconds, but their initial flashes often disappear before conventional telescopes can turn towards them.

Swift was designed to overcome that problem.

It carried three instruments: the Burst Alert Telescope, an X-ray Telescope and an Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope.

The Burst Alert Telescope continuously watched large areas of the sky for sudden flashes of gamma rays. Once it detected a burst, the spacecraft could automatically turn towards the source and examine the fading light using its other two telescopes.

It could also send the location to observatories on Earth, allowing astronomers around the world to begin their own observations.

The entire process typically took about a minute.

“Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more,” said S. Bradley Cenko, the mission’s principal investigator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.

“Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out. This typically took Swift about a minute to do.”

That speed changed the way astronomers studied sudden events in the universe.
Before Swift, scientists often knew that an enormous explosion had occurred but struggled to locate it quickly enough to investigate what had caused it.

Swift helped turn those brief flashes into events that could be studied in detail.

A remarkable record of discoveries

During its long career, Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and studied over 1,400 supernova explosions.

It also witnessed stars being torn apart by black holes, monitored active galaxies and examined asteroids and comets closer to Earth.

Its observations contributed to approximately 7,000 published scientific papers.
One of its most important early discoveries came in May 2005, just months after the spacecraft began operating.

Swift detected the afterglow of an exceptionally brief gamma-ray burst designated GRB 050509B.
The initial burst lasted only 0.03 seconds, yet Swift turned towards its location quickly enough to detect 11 X-ray photons from the fading event.

It was the first time astronomers had detected an afterglow from such a short gamma-ray burst.
The discovery provided important evidence supporting theories that these brief explosions could result from collisions between neutron stars.

Such stars can contain more mass than the Sun compressed into an object roughly the size of a city.
Swift’s ability to respond rapidly also made it useful for studying unexpected events that were not part of its original mission.

Scientists could request observations of newly discovered objects and, in some cases, have the spacecraft begin examining them within minutes.

Its flexible scheduling system could accommodate as many as 75 separate targets in a day.
John Nousek, the mission’s operations director and a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Pennsylvania State University, credited the spacecraft’s responsiveness and the teams operating it.
“The unique speed of response of the Swift hardware, the extraordinary success of the rapid mission operations, and the closely knit teamwork of the Swift Flight and Science Operations teams placed Swift at the crossroads of burgeoning areas of research,” he said.

The spacecraft was originally led by astronomer Neil Gehrels, whose work helped establish its scientific approach. NASA renamed the observatory in his honour in 2018, following his death.

How the attempt to save Swift unfolded

Swift’s scientific instruments were still functioning when its orbit began deteriorating more rapidly than expected.

The problem was not a failure of its telescopes but the atmosphere surrounding Earth.

Even hundreds of kilometres above the planet, traces of atmospheric gases remain. Satellites moving through this thin atmosphere experience drag, which gradually reduces their orbital altitude.

Recent solar activity made the situation worse.

When the Sun becomes more active, it can heat Earth’s upper atmosphere, causing it to expand. Satellites at low altitudes then encounter greater atmospheric resistance.

Swift began losing altitude at an increasing rate.

NASA and commercial spacecraft company Katalyst Space attempted to address the problem through an ambitious robotic servicing mission.

Katalyst developed a spacecraft called LINK, designed to approach Swift and potentially raise its orbit, extending the observatory’s operational life.

Such a manoeuvre would have been particularly challenging because Swift was not originally designed for robotic servicing.

The mission also offered an opportunity to demonstrate technologies that could eventually allow spacecraft to be repositioned or serviced in orbit rather than abandoned when their useful lives approached an end.

However, the rescue did not proceed as planned.

NASA said attitude-control problems with LINK led the agency and Katalyst to scale back the mission in August without attempting to raise Swift’s orbit.

Attitude control refers to a spacecraft’s ability to maintain and adjust its orientation in space, a critical requirement when approaching another satellite.

Despite the setback, LINK continued demonstrating its technology.

In early September, NASA reported that the vehicle had deployed all three of its robotic arms and operated its three electric propulsion thrusters simultaneously.

It also adjusted its orbit to approach Swift, coming within approximately 12 to 15 kilometres.
The servicing spacecraft did not attempt a closer approach.

The tests provided data for future robotic servicing missions, but Swift remained in its declining orbit.

One final return to science

Following the unsuccessful rescue effort, NASA allowed Swift to resume its astronomical observations.

Scientists had previously suspended much of its work to reduce atmospheric drag and preserve the spacecraft’s altitude while the servicing mission was being prepared.

Returning to normal observations meant the spacecraft would again turn towards different astronomical targets, increasing drag and accelerating its descent.

Nevertheless, Swift continued examining the universe.

During its final weeks, it observed hundreds of targets, including the remains of stellar explosions, active supermassive black holes in distant galaxies and comets travelling through the solar system.
On 20 October, the observatory reached an altitude of approximately 275 kilometres.

At that height, it could no longer maintain the stability needed for scientific observations.

The spacecraft entered safe mode, a protective operating condition intended to safeguard essential systems when normal operations cannot continue.

Controllers at Pennsylvania State University then transmitted a command that effectively ended the mission and prepared the spacecraft for re-entry.

After almost 22 years, Swift had made its final astronomical observation.

The command came from the same Pennsylvania State University operations team that had helped keep Swift working, far beyond the two-year mission NASA originally planned.

Where will the telescope fall?

The precise location of Swift’s re-entry remains uncertain.

The US Space Force is tracking the spacecraft as its orbit continues to decay, with current predictions placing its return around 6 November.

However, forecasting the exact time and location of an uncontrolled re-entry is difficult.
Small changes in atmospheric density, solar activity and the spacecraft’s orientation can alter how quickly it loses altitude.

Swift’s orbit passes over a band of Earth extending approximately 21 degrees north and south of the equator.

That includes large stretches of ocean as well as parts of Africa, India, Southeast Asia, Australia and Central and South America.

Being beneath the spacecraft’s orbital path does not mean a particular location will be struck by debris.

As Swift descends into the denser atmosphere, it will experience intense heating and aerodynamic forces.

Its solar panels, antennas and other exposed structures are likely to break apart before the main body disintegrates.

Most of the spacecraft’s aluminium structure, electronics and other components are expected to burn up.

However, denser and more heat-resistant objects, including some internal mechanical components and telescope materials, could survive.

The observatory used reaction wheels to control its orientation. These spinning devices allowed the spacecraft to turn accurately towards astronomical targets without constantly firing thrusters.
Such dense components are among those that could potentially withstand part of the descent.
Any surviving debris is considered more likely to fall into the ocean than onto populated land, although its eventual location cannot yet be established.

NASA’s October mission statements did not provide a detailed public assessment of the risk from surviving Swift debris.

The agency’s orbital debris safety standards generally require spacecraft to limit the expected risk of human casualty from re-entry debris.

A mission that will continue helping astronomers

Although Swift’s instruments have fallen silent, the information they collected will remain available to scientists.

NASA says the observatory leaves behind approximately 12 terabytes of scientific data, including more than 1.5 million images captured by its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope.

The archive also contains over two decades of brightness measurements, spectra and observations of astronomical events.

Researchers will be able to revisit these records as new discoveries and improved analytical techniques help them answer questions that were not possible to address when the observations were first made.

Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s Astrophysics Division, said the spacecraft had far exceeded expectations.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” he said.
He added that Swift had helped establish rapid-response observations as an important part of modern astronomy.

NASA is now examining how existing telescopes, commercial space capabilities and possible new missions could help fill the gap left by Swift.

More than five years after the fall of Kabul, the US Air Force is finally mothballing its small fleet of A-29 (EMB 314) Super Tucanos.

The USAF acquired the aircraft as part of its efforts to equip the former Afghan Air Force, but then struggled to find a role for them after that mission ended.

USAF retires A-29 Super Tucano, contracting SNC for storage

The US Air Force has divested its fleet of three Embraer A-29 Super Tucano advanced trainer/light attack aircraft according to a new contract.

The development comes two years after the Air Force took the aircraft to the Air Force Test Pilot School.

On the 29 October, the Air Force released a notice that it would award a sole-source contract to SNC to provide on-call support for the aircraft while in storage.

The three fully sealed Super Tucanos currently in storage at Edwards Air Force Base are not expected to return to flight for the Air Force.

SNC is to ensure the aircraft’s safe storage, environmental compliance, and ground movement within the installation. This concerns factors like oil leaks.

The US was heavily involved in Embraer’s Super Tucano

The A-29 was developed by Brazil’s Embraer, but the US became an important part of its international production and marketing effort through a partnership between Embraer and Sierra Nevada Corporation.

A second production line was set up in the US. US aircraft and those exported by the US to countries like Afghanistan (pre-2021) were built in the US, not Brazil.

Over 260 examples had been delivered by 2023. Brazil is the largest operator with 99 aircraft purchased, while Colombia, Chile, and Ecuador are significant operators.

The US government procured 26 A-29s for Afghanistan, although not all had been delivered to the Afghan Air Force when the Taliban returned to power.

Embraer continues to see modest international orders and deliveries for the aircraft.

Uruguay renews light attack capabilities with arrival of 1st Embraer A-29B Super Tucanos Uruguay renews light attack capabilities with arrival of 1st Embraer A-29B Super Tucanos

The effort to support pre-2021 Afghanistan

The Super Tucano’s use in the USAF was closely tied to supporting US allies, particularly Afghanistan, in counter-insurgency operations.

The USAF never operated the A-29 as a conventional operational light attack squadron, even though it was heavily involved in developing and supporting the aircraft.

USAF A-29s weren’t really bought to equip an American combat unit. Instead, they were part of an effort to build an Afghan fixed-wing attack capability.

Moody AFB was selected in 2014 as the training base, and the 81st Fighter Squadron was then established. The first of 20 A-29s arrived in September 2014, with the first Afghan pilots graduating in late 2015 and initial deliveries to Afghanistan in 2016.

The USAF purchased a tiny flight of A-29s in 2020-2021 for experimentation and a foreign advisory mission.

For a period, the USAF became interested in the A-29 (and AT-6 Wolverine) as the Light Attack Experiment, with the idea being it could be used on missions where the F-15, F-16, or A-10 were excessive.

By 2022, the aircraft no longer suited the USAF’s operational missions, and it planned to dispose of them.

In 2024, rather than disposing of them, it decided to transfer them to the Air Force Test Pilot School for flight-test training, spin testing, and sensors/weapons research.

At the time, it seemed like the A-29 had found a second life in the USAF. But this has evidently been short-lived, with the type now retiring.

In any accident investigation, locating the so-called ‘black box’ can provide crucial details to help piece together the sequence of events.

The aircraft black box is actually two devices: the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and the flight data recorder (FDR). Larger airlines need to have both installed.

But in the case of the fatal Learjet 60 crash in Florida, the rules around these black boxes are more opaque.

In the first press conference since the tragedy, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) member Tom Chapman explained that the aircraft’s maintenance records suggested a CVR, at least, was installed.

“Our indication early here from aircraft maintenance records is that a cockpit voice recorder was installed on this aircraft,” he said.

“What we don’t know is whether that recorder was still on board; sometimes these things change over time.”

The NTSB said that the Learjet had potentially begun breaking up before impacting the ground, but refrained from speculating as to any possible cause. Chapman admitted that due to the high speeds involved, recovering meaningful parts would be a “real challenge.”

With a substantial part of the wreckage buried in a crater that is now filled with water, locating a data recorder could be vital to discovering what went wrong.

Did the Learjet carry the important ‘black box’ recorders?

During the press conference, Chapman confirmed that the Learjet was operated by Aurora Aviation, doing business as Upper Jets. It is a Part 135 operator, offering private jet flights on-demand.

Unlike commercial airlines, which operate under the FAA’s Part 121 rules, Part 135 operators are not always required to have both black boxes installed. For example, the FDR, which records flight parameters such as altitude and speed, is generally only required in aircraft with ten or more seats.

A previous sales listing for N722BD, the Learjet 60 involved in the crash, shows an eight-passenger layout inside. That puts it below the threshold required for a mandatory FDR, although some operators install them voluntarily.

However, Part 135 operators do require a cockpit voice recorder, or CVR, on multiengine turbine aircraft configured with six or more passenger seats when two pilots are required. The Learjet 60 does require two pilots.

As the NTSB stated, the aircraft’s maintenance records indicated it did have a CVR installed, and the sales listing also mentions a Universal CVR-30 cockpit voice recorder among its equipment. But it’s possible that it was subsequently removed before the accident.

“We’re still seeking to determine whether there was a recorder, and then of course we’re very hopeful that we can recover it,” Chapman explained. “It’s too early to know, but that’ll be very important data.”

Could a cockpit voice recorder survive the impact?

The Learjet crash was one of the most violent aviation incidents in recent memory. The speeds involved bent asphalt on impact and created a huge crater in the ground. The aircraft fragmented into thousands of tiny parts, which a team is now attempting to round up and recover.

Not all the debris is near the crater, however, with much spread around the neighbourhood, making progress laborious. Speaking at the media briefing, senior investigator Timothy Monville said of the crash site,

“I’m getting conflicting information. It’s probably a half mile by four tenths of a mile. But it’s scattered among ball fields, businesses, personal residences, and the debris is rather small.”

If the aircraft did carry a CVR, even a devastating crash such as this does not mean all data has been lost forever. Cockpit voice recorders are designed to protect their recordings against severe impact and fire. Even extensive damage to the recorder’s outer casing does not necessarily mean its contents are destroyed.

Nevertheless, questions remain over whether it was even on board at the time of the crash, and locating it is going to be a tough job.

“We’ll be better off with it,” Chapman admitted. “But even without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”

The Florida Learjet 60 crash highlights questions investigators must examine.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Thunderstorms can extend above cruising altitude, exposing aircraft to powerful air currents, turbulence and icing hazards.
  • Airframe icing, ice-crystal icing and Mach tuck are distinct phenomena; none has been established as the cause of the Learjet crash.
  • The crew reported icing, turbulence and overspeed, but investigators must determine how the emergency developed and whether weather contributed.

The crew of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on 1 November reported icing, turbulence and increasing precipitation before the aircraft entered a steep descent, killing all nine people aboard.

The jet was flying from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. According to Flightradar24’s review of air traffic control recordings, the crew requested a climb from around 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet before reporting a rapid descent and an overspeed condition.

Weather analysis published by MyRadar places a developing thunderstorm near the aircraft’s flight path. Its analysis suggests the storm grew from approximately 33,000 feet to 48,300 feet between 12:36 p.m. and 12:56 p.m., a period spanning the accident.

We’ve reviewed radar and temperature data surrounding the crash of N722BD. This loop depicts the rapid vertical development of a convective cell, which lofted plentiful moisture. The aircraft entered this cell at 12:47-48 p.m., encountering severe icing and turbulence. https://t.co/7qzeOsLAYO

— MyRadar Weather (@MyRadarWX) November 2, 2026

Those measurements do not establish the storm’s precise height when the Learjet encountered it. They do, however, illustrate why cruising altitude does not necessarily put an aircraft above the weather.

How thunderstorms affect aircraft at cruising altitude

Thunderstorms develop vertically, with powerful rising air currents carrying moisture high into the atmosphere. Their tops can extend above the cruising altitudes of commercial airliners and business jets.

Within and around these clouds, aircraft can encounter turbulence, strong updrafts and downdrafts, hail and icing. Rapid changes in airflow can alter an aircraft’s airspeed, angle of attack and flight path, placing additional demands on its flight controls and crew.

In severe encounters, turbulence can cause substantial changes in attitude and altitude. Extreme turbulence can impose loads capable of damaging an aircraft. However, neither a nearby storm nor a subsequent dive establishes that structural damage occurred.

Weather radar also has limitations. It primarily detects precipitation rather than directly displaying every hazardous air movement. A weak return does not necessarily mean smooth or harmless conditions, particularly near the upper parts of a storm.

FAA guidance consequently emphasises avoiding thunderstorms, rather than using radar to find a route through them. Datalink weather imagery is intended for broader route planning, not close-range manoeuvring between rapidly changing storm cells.

Why icing can still threaten aircraft at altitude

Conventional airframe icing occurs when supercooled liquid droplets strike an aircraft and freeze. Clear ice forms when the water spreads before freezing, producing a relatively transparent deposit that can change the shape of an aerodynamic surface.

The resulting loss of performance is not simply about added weight. Ice can disrupt airflow, reduce lift, increase drag and cause a wing or tail surface to stall at a lower angle of attack than it would when clean.

At very low temperatures, however, the type of moisture matters. Below approximately −40°C, conventional supercooled-liquid-water icing becomes physically unlikely, and ice crystals become the more relevant concern.

Ice crystals generally do not accumulate on cold external surfaces in the same way as liquid droplets. But in high concentrations, they can partially melt and accumulate within warmer parts of turbine engines or affect heated sensors. They can also be difficult for conventional airborne weather radar to detect.

The Learjet crew’s icing report therefore warrants investigation, but it does not establish what accumulated, where it formed or whether it affected control.

What is Mach tuck, and how does it differ from icing?

Mach tuck is a high-speed aerodynamic effect, not a form of icing.

As an aircraft’s Mach number increases, airflow over parts of its wing can become supersonic even while the aircraft itself remains below the speed of sound. Shock waves develop, and changes in the pressure distribution can shift the wing’s effective lifting force rearwards, creating a nose-down pitching tendency.

Associated airflow separation can also produce buffet and affect handling. Aircraft are designed with operating limits and control systems to manage their high-speed characteristics, but exceeding those limits can make recovery more difficult.

The Learjet crew reported overspeed during the descent. That makes its speed history relevant, but overspeed alone does not establish that Mach tuck occurred, or whether excessive speed preceded or followed the initial loss of control.

NTSB investigation will examine the sequence

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating and is expected to provide an update at a briefing in West Palm Beach on 2 November.

Investigators will need to establish how the aircraft’s flight path, weather exposure and any aerodynamic or mechanical problems developed together. The crew’s reports and available tracking data describe a rapidly escalating emergency; they do not yet explain its cause.

]]> Ryanair warns airfares could rise 20% in 2027 as airline considers staff pay freeze https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ryanair-warns-airfares-could-rise-2027/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:19:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55279 Cheap flights could become harder to find next year, with Ryanair warning airfares across Europe may rise by up to 20% as airlines grapple with soaring fuel costs.

The post Ryanair warns airfares could rise 20% in 2027 as airline considers staff pay freeze appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Ryanair warns European airfares could rise 10-20% in 2027 as fuel hedges expire and costs surge.
  • Passengers are unlikely to see immediate increases, with Ryanair protected by fuel hedges until March 2027.
  • Ryanair may freeze staff pay and expand AI use as Europe's airlines face higher fuel bills.

Europe’s largest airline says all carriers face significantly higher fuel bills in 2027 as low-cost fuel hedges expire and jet fuel prices remain elevated. Ryanair warned passengers should prepare for “double-digit” fare increases next year, with chief executive Michael O’Leary describing the situation as a “very significant cost cliff”.

Today (2 November), the airline reported a 15% fall in half-year profit despite carrying a record 125.8 million passengers, with higher fuel costs and lower fares both having an impact.

Chief executive Michael O’Leary said the airline is now reviewing all its costs – including considering temporary wage freezes for staff, and increased use of AI in back-office operations.

“There’s still no resolution in the Middle East.” O’Leary told CNBC. “Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. This is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year.” 

And he warned ticket prices across Europe could rise by up to 20% next year as airlines pass on at least some of the higher fuel bill to passengers.

Why are fares expected to rise?

Ryanair says fuel prices are likely to remain elevated because of the continuing conflict in the Middle East.

“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said O’Leary. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.” 

Ryanair warned that “all EU airlines face a significantly higher fuel bill next year” as cheaper fuel hedges expire.

What does this mean for passengers?

Nothing immediately.

The airline said current-year earnings remain largely protected because 80% of its fuel requirement is hedged at lower prices through March 2027. The bigger impact is likely to be felt next summer and beyond, when today’s lower-cost fuel contracts have expired.

Ryanair believes industry-wide aircraft shortages, ongoing engine supply problems and a lack of short-haul capacity could give airlines more room to push through fare increases.

O’Leary said: “I believe you’re going to see airfares rise next year across Europe by 10%, maybe even 20%.”

Staff face pay freeze

Passengers are not the only ones being warned about the impact of higher fuel prices.

Ryanair said it is reviewing costs across the business, including “maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes)”.

The airline is also examining “lower crewing ratios” and “increased use of AI to drive further operational and back-office/support functions productivity” as it looks for ways to offset rising costs.

However, the Unite union said it had a multiyear pay deal in place that covered 2027.

“Unite hasn’t been advised of any such proposals and we have a multiyear pay deal in place which covers next year,” Oliver Richardson, a national officer at the union told The Guardian.

There’s no suggestion of job cuts, and Ryanair continues to grow. The airline expects to carry more than 220 million passengers next year and says its first Boeing MAX 10 aircraft will enter service in spring 2027.

]]> Greenland completes hat-trick as Ilulissat Airport opens as third international gateway https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ilulissat-airport-greenland-airports/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:15:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55119 Air Greenland operates inaugural international flight into Ilulissat Airport, the third and final airport to open under Greenland Airport's expansion programme.

The post Greenland completes hat-trick as Ilulissat Airport opens as third international gateway appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Danish Transport Authority has approved the opening of a new international airport in Ilulissat, completing Greenland’s airport expansion programme.

The inaugural international flight from Copenhagen, operated by Air Greenland, touched down at Ilulissat International Airport on Thursday 29 October. The aircraft was an Airbus A330neo, marking the start of a new era for Greenland’s tourism and aviation sector. Operations and opening hours at the airport are now expected to ramp up gradually, with the aim of full operations by the summer season of 2027.

“Hundreds of people have worked hard to ensure that we can now complete a historic expansion of Greenland’s infrastructure,” said Jens Lauridsen, CEO of Greenland Airports.

The airport’s opening comes as Lauridsen is due to step down as CEO at the end of October.

Why the opening of Ilulissat matters

Known as the City of Icebergs, Ilulissat sits on Greenland’s west coast, more than 550km north of the capital, Nuuk. It is Greenland’s third-largest city and is the gateway to the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Ilulissat Icefjord.

Until now, access has been tricky. International travellers had to arrive by cruise ship or connect through one of Greenland’s other air transport hubs. The old airport relied on a short 854m runway, which limited the types of aircraft that could land there.

The new airport changes that. Lauridsen said it would “fundamentally change how the country is connected and how Greenland is connected to the outside world.” For local residents and businesses, it promises shorter journeys, better connections and more efficient cargo operations. It also fits the island government’s efforts to grow tourism and diversify an economy that relies heavily on fishing.

Tourism bodies have warned that the town now needs to be ready for the extra visitors. Air Greenland plans to use a Jettime-operated Boeing 737-800 for its winter service to the airport, and from spring 2027 it will operate a narrowbody A320neo on the route.

The third and final piece in Greenland Airport’s expansion puzzle

Ilulissat follows the opening of Qaqortoq in April this year and Nuuk serving the capital in November 2024. Together, the three airports form the backbone of Greenland’s aviation infrastructure, which Lauridsen described as a “long-term investment.”

Notably, Danish authorities approved security at Ilulissat without restrictions. However, Lauridsen cautioned that the work is far from over. “The work doesn’t stop because we have opened the doors,” he said, pointing to efforts to train staff, optimise resources and strengthen cross-functional cooperation to ensure well-functioning operations and a good passenger experience.

Nuuk’s new airport set to be a game changer for Greenland (United Kingdom) Nuuk’s new airport set to be a game changer for Greenland (United Kingdom)

With opportunity comes risk

The new airport brings risks as well as opportunities. Earlier this year, Aerospace Global News reported that Air Greenland has struggled with moving its main hub from Kangerlussuaq to the capital Nuuk. Adapting to the new operating environment proved costly and the airline posted a much steeper loss for the first half of 2025.

Severe weather and infrastructure teething problems also added to the airline’s difficulties. Delays in commissioning of the new airport, icy runway conditions, baggage and fuelling issues and shortages of spare parts led to 59 cancellations of jet aircraft flights in the first half of 2025.

That experience gives added weight to Lauridsen’s warning that work doesn’t stop just because the doors have now opened.

Ilulissat will test whether the lessons from Nuuk have been learned, particularly as operations ramp up through the winter, when Greenland’s weather is at its harshest. The phased opening and use of a leased Boeing 737-800 on Air Greenland’s route this winter suggest a cautious approach and the phased opening hints at efforts to avoid the growing pains seen in the capital.
